channel.title: The Brief — Adam's News
channel.description: Every story from Adam's three daily briefs (9 AM / 5 PM / 10 PM CT) as its own item, readable right in your feed reader, with a link to the original article.

item.title: Ukraine hit Russia's rocket-fuel factory overnight — while Russian strikes left 280,000 households without power
item.description:
Ukraine's long-range campaign moved from refineries to the munitions chain itself overnight. According to Ukraine's General Staff, reported by the Kyiv Independent via Europe Says, Ukrainian attack drones and Neptune cruise missiles hit the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, in Russia's Rostov region, overnight on October 31. The General Staff says a finished-goods warehouse caught fire and four production workshops were damaged. The plant makes solid rocket propellant for the Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as other missile and aircraft weapons, and it has been sanctioned by the EU, UK and US for its role in the war. The same night, Ukraine says it also hit four Russian military supply depots in occupied Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Luhansk regions.
Russia has not commented on the Kamensky claim itself — Rostov Governor Yuri Slyusar acknowledged an overnight air attack on Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and four other districts but said nothing about the plant — and the Kyiv Independent notes it could not independently verify the military's claims. That caveat matters, but the plant's role is not in dispute: OSINT project Varta, cited by Militarnyi, describes it as one of the largest chemical plants in southern Russia, producing gunpowder, explosives and ammunition components, and it was already hit by a drone strike on August 24. The General Staff's argument is straightforward: hitting solid rocket propellant production reduces Russia's ability to shell Ukrainian towns with multiple-launch rocket systems. Moscow's side of that argument, repeated throughout the war, is that Ukrainian strikes on its industry are attacks on its war economy — and its own overnight claims ran in the other direction, with the Defence Ministry saying it intercepted 433 Ukrainian drones over 19 regions and struck Kyiv's CHP-6 plant, Kharkiv industrial workshops and a cargo ship off Odesa.
The other half of the night was the toll on Ukrainian civilians. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian strikes left around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region and more than 80,000 in the Kyiv region without electricity — about 280,000 in total — after hits on a combined heat and power plant in Kyiv, four electrical substations and a gas facility in Dnipropetrovsk, a power plant in Shostka, and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv. Kyiv's mayor had already confirmed three drone strikes on CHP-6 on Friday night, and on Saturday evening a 12-year-old girl was injured in Kyiv's Obolon district when debris from a projectile fell on a shopping centre, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration. Ukraine's General Staff counted 173 engagements on Saturday, heaviest around Kostyantynivka and Pokrovsk. This is the third night in a row of the resumed deep-strike campaign — Novokuibyshevsk on Thursday night, the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Ufa on Friday night, Kamensky now — and it comes as winter approaches, when power outages stop being an inconvenience and start being a survival issue.
In short: Ukraine says it damaged a key rocket-propellant plant and four supply depots overnight, Russia claims a huge drone interception and its own strikes on Kyiv's power plant, and the confirmed civilian cost is 280,000 households without power plus a child injured in Kyiv — the energy war and the munitions war now running in parallel.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Iran says Hormuz could reopen in two days — but only on its terms, and Washington hasn't agreed to them
item.description:
The most consequential diplomatic development of the day is also the most conditional. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday that talks with Qatari mediators have produced a proposal cutting the implementation time for Iran's plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to two days — down from a Qatari suggestion of five. But the plan comes with Tehran's full list of conditions attached: lifting sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum, reducing US forces in the region, restoring oil waivers, releasing all of Iran's frozen funds including money held in Qatar, and recognition of the shipping routes Iran discussed with Oman, with other routes closed. Araghchi called a letter from US Vice President JD Vance "a positive step" toward dialogue, then immediately added that Iran sees "no need to meet with the Americans at this stage" and dismissed reports of a meeting as "media speculation."
That directly tempers the other Saturday reporting. The Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, cited by The Media Line, reported that an American delegation is expected in Doha after more than 12 hours of Qatari-Iranian talks in Tehran produced preliminary understandings on Iran's nuclear programme, Hormuz navigation and financial incentives, with China and Russia expected as guarantors. A separate draft framework reported by Al Arabiya English goes further, suggesting Iran's highly enriched uranium stockpile could be transferred to a third country or reduced in enrichment, with Hormuz reopening within seven days of an initial understanding. Neither government has publicly confirmed any of this, and an Axios correspondent cited by Iran International said Tehran and Washington have not agreed to resume direct talks. An Iranian delegation is in Doha, but according to the Revolutionary Guards-linked Tasnim agency, it is there to advance talks with Qatar, not to negotiate with US officials.
Meanwhile the strait itself stayed dangerous. UKMTO reported a tanker struck near Iran's Lavan Island on Saturday; Iran's Revolutionary Guards said it hit a mine after using an "unauthorised route." On Friday, UKMTO reported a small boat attaching limpet mines to a tanker, causing an engine-room fire — described by Reuters via CNBC as the first known successful limpet-mine strike in the waterway since the war began in February. And the market has already priced in the risk: Brent's December contract settled Friday at $117.64 a barrel, up 2.4%, its highest since late April, with the January contract at $113.43; WTI settled at $104.12. Brent finished October up 13.6% and WTI up 15.2%. US average regular gas was about $4.18 a gallon on Saturday, according to AAA, cited by US Brief.
For ordinary people, the gap between the two stories is the whole story. A two-day reopening on Iran's terms would ease fuel prices fast; a failed mediation, three days before the US midterms on November 3, leaves the post-election military option that both sides have been warning about squarely on the table. OPEC+ meets online on Sunday, which may add its own signal before markets reopen.
In short: Iran says Hormuz could reopen in two days if the US lifts sanctions, pulls back forces and frees frozen funds — but says there are no plans to meet US officials yet, reports of a Doha breakthrough are unconfirmed by either government, and oil just closed October at its highest since April.
Sources:
Source: themedialine.org.

item.title: The US ordered its non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia as Houthi drones kept coming — four intercepted in a day
item.description:
The US Mission to Saudi Arabia disclosed on Friday that it has ordered the departure of non-emergency government employees and their families from Saudi Arabia, an order that took effect on October 23, citing safety risks from Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure that have caused casualties and major travel disruptions. US government staff must now get special authorisation to use Saudi airports. The embassy noted Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has partially reopened, while Jeddah and Dammam remain operational with some delays and cancellations. The order is the clearest public US signal yet of how seriously Washington takes the Houthi campaign — even as the US has held off its own strikes since the May 2025 ceasefire.
The attacks behind it continued through Saturday. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted four Houthi drones over Medina, Riyadh, and southern and eastern Saudi Arabia on October 30–31, according to coalition spokesperson Turki al Maliki, reported by ISW. The Houthis denied on October 30 that they targeted Medina and have not claimed responsibility for these drone attacks. On the ground in Yemen, government-aligned forces repelled Houthi advances along the Taiz–Aden road in Lahij on October 30–31 with Saudi close air support, and recaptured high ground overlooking al Hazm in Jawf. A separate investigation by Geneva firm AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence, reported by Europe Says, claims Russian satellites were observed over Saudi military and energy targets before and after Houthi strikes — a single-source claim worth noting, not yet corroborated, and it does not change the immediate picture for travellers: airports disrupted, an evacuation order in force, and no sign the drone campaign is slowing.
In short: Washington has formally pulled its non-essential people out of Saudi Arabia, the coalition says it downed four Houthi drones in a day, and fighting inside Yemen is heating up along the Taiz–Aden road — while a claim of Russian satellite help for Houthi targeting remains unverified.
Sources:
Source: cumhuriyetdaily.com.

item.title: Nvidia showed a co-packaged optics prototype at SEMICON West:
item.description:
Nvidia unveiled its OOI co-packaged optics hardware prototype in San Francisco, aimed at future high-performance computing architectures, with its Feynman architecture (slated for 2028) as the launchpad — but mass production is not expected until after 2030, so this is a roadmap signal, not a product.
Source:
Source: wisevoter.com.

item.title: Friday's AI selloff, in context:
item.description:
Friday was the Nasdaq's worst day since June (-2.86%), Alphabet fell 12.64% in its biggest one-day drop since its 2004 listing, and Intel fell 28.58% in its worst day since 1974 — the rotation that put Apple back ahead of Nvidia as the world's most valuable company ($5.03T).
A market story, not a product story, but it explains the week's tech headlines. Source:
Source: techtrendsnewsupdate.substack.com.

item.title: AiSOC — open-source SOC with AI agents, v20.4.0:
item.description:
AiSOC is a self-hosted Security Operations Center under the MIT licence: it collects logs, correlates them into incidents and hands them to AI agents that record every prompt and tool call.
Started May 2026, it counts 5,489 stars and 561 forks as of October 31, with v20.4.0 out that day. Worth a look for a home lab or small SOC; note there is no independent security audit on record, and the version number has raced from 8.1.0 in September to 20.4.0, which says more about release pace than maturity.
Source:
Source: pasqualepillitteri.it.

item.title: MiniCPM-OCR — open document-parsing models:
item.description:
ModelBest and OpenBMB open-sourced the MiniCPM-OCR series on October 31: MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 (1.3B) and MiniCPM-OCR Jev (2B) for document parsing and parsing-quality assessment, on GitHub, Hugging Face and ModelScope, with vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and Ollama support plus fine-tuning code.
Useful if you scan or parse documents locally instead of sending them to a cloud API. Source:
Source: morningstar.com.

item.title: Binance says 90% of the $6.3B theft is replaced; withdrawals targeted for Sunday:
item.description:
Binance says it has replenished 90% of the cryptocurrency stolen on Thursday (up from ~80%), with its top 10 user assets — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD and ZEC — now fully backed at 100%, funded from corporate treasury, its futures insurance fund and a partial SAFU deployment expected within 24 hours.
Withdrawals, paused since the hack, are on track to reopen in phases on Sunday, November 1, subject to security checks. A new proof-of-reserves snapshot (balances at midnight UTC October 31) shows 100%+ coverage for those tokens, but the full cryptographic proof users can independently verify is not due until November 3 — so Sunday's reopening comes before outside verification.
Sources:
Source: Www.coindesk.com.

item.title: Oracle E-Business Suite flaw now seeing exploitation attempts:
item.description:
CVE-2026-101767 (CVSS 9.8) lets someone with no login run SQL as the main APPS database user and then run commands on the server.
Oracle fixed it in its October 20 Critical Patch Update; a week later, decoy servers started catching attackers trying it, and Shadowserver counts more than 670 internet-facing EBS instances. If you run EBS, this is the patch — it is not yet in CISA's KEV catalog as of October 31.
Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: China-linked Vapor Panda used an open-source AI pentest tool against 200+ organisations:
item.description:
CrowdStrike reports that the state-backed group Vapor Panda used the ARTEX agentic AI penetration-testing framework (paired mainly with DeepSeek and a second commercial model) to target more than 200 organisations across at least 14 countries since October 17, with about 140 showing compromise or moderate-confidence intrusion evidence in 11 days.
Victims include foreign ministries, a European presidency and prime minister's office, defence/intelligence agencies, 19 US organisations in pharma, semiconductors, defence, nuclear and finance, and telecoms in the US, Belgium and the Philippines. The campaign is still active — and it is a case study in why an open-source offensive tool cuts both ways.
Source:
Source: cyberrecaps.com.

item.title: Backdoored Claude Code extension reached up to 5,000 developers:
item.description:
A malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension (versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313) appeared in Cursor's extension marketplace for roughly 11 hours on October 29 and was downloaded by at most 5,000 users across Windows, macOS and Linux.
The tampered package was not built or published by Anthropic — an attacker gained access to publish it under the legitimate extension identity. If you installed or updated Claude Code in Cursor around October 29, verify your extension version.
Source:
Source: cyberrecaps.com.

item.title: TeamViewer flaw lets the supported computer attack the technician + Android "SMS of Death" PoC:
item.description:
TeamViewer CVE-2026-111585 (CVSS 8.8, fixed in 15.83) reverses the usual direction — the computer being supported can attack the technician who connects to it.
Separately, a public proof of concept for an Android "SMS of Death" (CVE-2026-58882) that crashes unpatched phones went public on October 31. Patch both.
Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: The energy war escalated on both sides overnight — Kyiv lost power and water, a giant Russian refinery complex caught fire
item.description:
Russia and Ukraine traded energy strikes overnight, and both sides' claims point to a sharp escalation rather than a one-off exchange. According to a daily war brief compiling Ukrainian official statements, Russian forces struck Kyiv's critical infrastructure with drones overnight, hitting a facility three times and cutting electricity and water to multiple districts; Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed a critical infrastructure facility was hit, with outages reported in Troyeshchyna, Obolon, Pechersk and several other districts, and parts of the city also left without water. Kharkiv took Shahed-type drone hits across three districts, injuring three people and damaging ten residential buildings, according to mayor Ihor Terekhov. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 134 drones, including 72 jet-powered Shahed models, hitting a combined heat and power plant in Kyiv, four electrical substations and a gas facility in Dnipropetrovsk, and another power plant in Shostka, with railway infrastructure damaged in Dnipro and Kharkiv.
Russia's Defence Ministry, for its part, said its air defences intercepted 433 Ukrainian drones overnight over 19 Russian regions, and claimed its own drone strikes hit Kyiv's CHP-6 power plant, workshops in Kharkiv's Proton industrial zone, and a cargo ship off Odesa. Moscow describes CHP-6 as supplying electricity to military logistics and weapons storage; Kyiv has consistently said Russian strikes on its energy system target civilian infrastructure ahead of winter, and Ukrainian officials had not publicly confirmed the specific Russian claims at the time of writing. Neither side's battlefield figures can be independently verified, and both regularly publish claims the other disputes — but the Kyiv outages are confirmed by the city's own mayor, which is the part that matters for people on the ground.
The other half of the night played out deep inside Russia. The Bashneft-Novoil oil refinery in Ufa, central Russia, caught fire Saturday after a reported Ukrainian drone attack, according to Russian outlet ASTRA, citing open-source analysis of eyewitness photos. ASTRA's analyst said a key catalytic reforming unit, the L-35 — which produces reformate, a high-octane gasoline component, and hydrogen needed to refine motor fuels — was likely burning. Residents reported several explosions Saturday morning, a column of smoke, and internet disruptions after an overnight drone alert, and Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported fires at two of the three refineries in Ufa's northern industrial zone. Bashneft's three adjacent Ufa refineries form one of Russia's largest refining complexes, with a combined capacity of 23.5 million tons of crude a year; Ukraine's General Staff said it hit the same L-35 unit in August 2025.
This is the second night of the resumed refinery campaign, not the first. Ukraine struck the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in the Samara region early Friday, ending a roughly two-week pause that followed heavy pressure from the Trump administration, and Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed Friday that three oil refineries and one gas-chemical complex were attacked overnight, with two men killed in Samara. Novak warned the strikes "could certainly lead to a reduction in supply volumes" under the diesel deal struck with President Donald Trump, which saw Russia ship about 510,000 tons of diesel in October. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters Tuesday that Ukrainian forces "do not have an order" not to hit refineries, and European allies had advised Kyiv to wait until after the US midterms — advice Kyiv now appears to have set aside.
For ordinary people, the two directions of this exchange land differently. In Kyiv, it is another winter morning of no power and no water in several districts, with private energy provider DTEK saying the capital was suffering electricity shortages again on Saturday after Friday's strikes on energy infrastructure. In Russia, a hit on a catalytic reforming unit at one of the country's biggest refining complexes is the kind of damage that can tighten domestic gasoline and diesel supply — which is exactly why the diesel deal with Washington is now in tension with the refinery campaign. The US-brokered energy ceasefire that briefly held in mid-October is now firmly in the past: Zelenskyy declared that pause over on October 15, and both sides have been hitting energy targets since.
In short: overnight brought confirmed power and water outages across Kyiv districts and a fire at the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Ufa, the second night of Ukraine's resumed refinery strikes — and with Moscow warning the strikes threaten the diesel volumes promised under its deal with Trump, the energy war is now running directly against the diplomacy meant to contain it.
Sources:
Source: app.osnt.in.

item.title: Hundreds of starving Oleshky residents arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday — the rare ceasefire held long enough to get them out
item.description:
Hundreds of people — and many pets — arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday afternoon after being evacuated from the frontline, Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, under a ceasefire that Pope Leo XIV called for and US First Lady Melania Trump helped to negotiate. CNN reports tearful reunions at an undisclosed border location, with evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags; President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the arrivals on Telegram, thanking Trump for the mediation and thanking "all journalists, all political and civic leaders, and all concerned people who drew global attention to the situation in Oleshky and the genuine humanitarian catastrophe" there.
The journey out was long by necessity. Access routes to Oleshky are heavily mined and littered with drone and vehicle debris, and crossing the Dnipro River directly into Ukrainian-controlled territory is not possible. After a two-day demining operation completed Thursday, residents who wanted to leave gathered Friday and travelled by bus through Crimea to Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar region, then flew to Gomel in Belarus — four planes in total, according to Ukrainian negotiator Davyd Arakhamia — before buses carried them to the Ukrainian border on Saturday. Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets travelled to Oleshky to personally escort the evacuees, becoming the first high-profile Ukrainian official to openly travel to occupied areas under Russian control since the start of the war. Relatives waited at the border with aid tents, coffee stands and provisions for the pets evacuees brought with them, and the director of the Chernihiv Regional Hospital, Andriy Zhydenko, was there with medical staff.
What they are coming out of is hard to overstate. Oleshky, in the Kherson region, has been occupied since 2022 and was hit by major flooding in 2023 after the Nova Kakhovka Dam collapsed. Ukrainian authorities reported the town ran out of food and other supplies in September, with no access to electricity, gas or medicine, and reports from that time said people were surviving on grass and weeds. CNN tells the story of one reunited couple, Dmytro and Larisa, separated for 1,711 days: Larisa, whose soldier husband made her vulnerable to the occupiers, lost a third of her body weight and now weighs just over 90 pounds. Zhydenko told CNN that prolonged malnutrition will be a key concern — evacuees will need to be fed carefully, because eating too much too quickly after starving for so long can itself be dangerous — and that the hospital was receiving people with injuries, stroke survivors and those with limited mobility.
The numbers are still deliberately vague. Around 2,000 residents were estimated to remain in Oleshky from a pre-war population of about 24,000, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv has specified how many people were evacuated; Melania Trump posted Friday that the convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people, and Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the exact number or the border crossing location. Some residents chose to travel to Russian-held territory instead — Russian media showed civilians arriving at a temporary accommodation site in Simferopol, Crimea — and others chose to stay, with replenished food and medical supplies promised. The truce, which AFP describes as the longest pause in fighting anywhere on the front line since Russia invaded in February 2022, began at 3am Tuesday and is due to end Sunday evening. It has held without violations so far, according to both Ukrainian and Russian officials.
In short: the Oleshky evacuation worked — hundreds of starving residents, some separated from family for years, are back in Ukraine after a Crimea–Anapa–Belarus odyssey — but the ceasefire that made it possible expires Sunday evening, and what happens to those who stayed behind depends on whether that local truce holds or collapses back into the wider war.
Sources:
Source: cnn.com.

item.title: Hormuz: Iran claims more tankers hit mines, the US disputes it — while Qatar pushes a deal that could bring US and Iranian officials face to face in Doha
item.description:
The Strait of Hormuz produced two conflicting stories on Friday, and both matter. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three oil tankers were halted after encountering "incidents" or hitting mines while using what Tehran calls an unauthorised southern route — two tankers stopped in the eastern and western parts of the strait, and later a supertanker carrying two million barrels of oil stopped after an explosion "after striking a naval mine," which the IRGC called "the third oil tanker to have exploded and caught fire today." That came a day after Iran's armed forces said at least four tankers had stopped in the area after hitting mines. Oman, meanwhile, said its navy rescued 25 sailors from the Panama-flagged merchant ship RITI after it was targeted and caught fire off Musandam, and UKMTO reported a separate vessel struck Friday by an unknown projectile 40 nautical miles south of Iran's Lavan Island, with the crew safe.
The US account directly contradicts Tehran's version. US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said in a video released Friday that US forces had "successfully cleared the strait's internationally recognised primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines," and that US forces remain present to keep those routes free and clear. CENTCOM rejected Iranian claims that commercial vessels were striking naval mines, and Qazinform notes the IRGC's claims have not been independently verified. The vessel counts do not line up neatly either — Ynet's reporting refers to one tanker hit and one other vessel on fire, while the IRGC's claims run to three or four — and none of the vessels in the IRGC's Friday claims was identified by name. What is independently confirmed is narrower: Oman did evacuate 25 crew from a burning vessel, UKMTO did log a projectile strike near Lavan Island, and oil markets moved — Brent crude climbed about 2% to $117.14 a barrel and WTI rose to $103.94, with UKMTO recording October as the month with the highest number of reported incidents in and around the strait since the war began on February 28.
Running alongside the shipping war is a diplomatic push with a deadline. Qatari mediators held more than 12 hours of talks in Tehran on Friday aimed at restarting direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran and preventing a renewed outbreak of war after the November 3 US midterm elections, according to Axios. The talks are expected to continue in Doha on Saturday, and the Times of Israel, citing the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, reports an American delegation is expected to join Iranian officials for direct talks in Doha following a reported breakthrough in indirect negotiations, with an understanding said to cover preliminary measures on Iran's nuclear programme, Hormuz navigation and financial incentives for Tehran, and China and Russia reportedly expected to serve as guarantors. Axios cautions that the two sides remain far apart on preconditions: the Trump administration wants nuclear concessions before talks resume, while Tehran insists Washington must first lift its naval blockade, release frozen funds and allow oil sales. Qatar is pushing reciprocal confidence-building steps over several days — Iran letting UN inspectors visit its bombed nuclear sites, met with some sanctions relief.
Inside the White House, the split is out in the open. Axios reports Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are sceptical a deal can be reached with Iran's current leadership and favour further weakening it, including additional strikes, while Vice President JD Vance and envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner favour resuming negotiations, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged giving sanctions pressure time to work. President Trump, speaking to reporters Friday, said "There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking... We have time, frankly. It's a war, but it is not a typical war," and separately told a Kansas City radio station the war would be "wrapped up soon," without saying how. Regional countries including Egypt, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have also urged Tehran to resume negotiations before the midterms, according to a regional source cited by Axios.
For ordinary people, the Hormuz standoff is already a wallet issue: Brent above $117 is the market pricing in the risk that the world's most important oil chokepoint stays contested, and the IEA's emergency oil and diesel releases earlier this month were a response to exactly this pressure. A Doha breakthrough would be the first direct US-Iran talks of this war; a failure, with the midterms three days away, leaves the post-election military option that both sides have been warning about squarely on the table.
In short: Iran claims three more tankers hit mines on an "unauthorised" route and the US says its cleared lanes are safe — the truth is unverified and the oil price is climbing — while Qatar's marathon Tehran talks may produce direct US-Iran talks in Doha as soon as Saturday, with Trump's own team split between negotiating and striking.
Sources:
Source: theleaders-online.com.

item.title: Israel's final election count confirms deadlock — 53 to 48, with a record 19 Arab-party seats and a foreign-interference probe clouding coalition talks
item.description:
Israel's Central Elections Committee released the final results on Friday, and they confirm what the late count suggested: no bloc has the 61 seats needed to govern the 120-seat Knesset. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud emerged as the largest single party with 27 seats, and his bloc holds 53; Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar took 21 seats, and his opposition bloc holds 48; Arab-led parties — the Joint List and Ra'am — took a record combined 19 seats. Turnout was 77.9%, with more than 5.7 million ballots cast. Netanyahu's bloc is down sharply from the 68 seats his coalition held in the outgoing Knesset.
What happens next runs through President Isaac Herzog. The committee is expected to submit the formal results to Herzog on November 4, after final checks, and the new Knesset is due to be sworn in on November 10. Herzog will consult party representatives before assigning the mandate to the candidate he believes is most likely to assemble 61 seats — not necessarily the leader of the largest party. CNN notes Eisenkot is likely to collect more recommendations than Netanyahu, since the Arab parties are expected to back him, and the chosen candidate gets 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension, to negotiate a government; if he fails, the mandate passes to another candidate, and if that fails too, the country goes to automatic elections. Netanyahu, as caretaker prime minister, has a built-in advantage in that sequence: if Eisenkot gets the mandate first and fails, Netanyahu can simply wait for his turn.
The arithmetic leaves three plausible paths, all awkward. One is a Netanyahu-led coalition picking up right-wing parties currently aligned with the opposition, such as Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad (12 seats) — though Bennett campaigned against Netanyahu. Another is an Eisenkot government relying on Arab-party support, which would reach 67 seats combined but which several opposition parties have ruled out; Eisenkot himself has not ruled it out under conditions, including recognising Israel as a Jewish state and Hamas as an extremist group. A third is a national unity government of Netanyahu and Eisenkot together, commanding around 66 seats. Netanyahu warned again on Friday against forming a coalition with Arab parties, calling such a partnership treasonous, while Yair Golan, leader of the smaller left-wing Democrats party, called for a government that would include them.
Hanging over the talks is an allegation neither side can yet prove or dismiss. Committee chair Justice Noam Sohlberg wrote to the Shin Bet that "serious suspicions" of foreign interference in the Arab vote had reached him, while saying he could not verify them; the Shin Bet said its inquiry does not "cast aspersions" on an entire population that voted lawfully. The dispute gives each camp a reason to harden its position just as the bargaining starts — and it lands on top of a record Arab turnout that many Palestinian citizens of Israel cast explicitly hoping to end Netanyahu's rule and remove far-right figures from his outgoing coalition, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
For ordinary Israelis, the practical consequence is weeks — possibly months — of caretaker government, with Netanyahu remaining in office throughout, while coalition talks decide whether the country gets a new government or another election. The Netanyahu trial remains on pause during this period, with no session during election week.
In short: the final count is 53–48–19 and nobody won — Netanyahu stays caretaker prime minister while Herzog's consultations, starting after November 4, decide whether Eisenkot, Netanyahu, or a unity deal can find 61 seats, with a record Arab bloc as kingmaker and an unverified interference allegation poisoning the talks before they start.
Sources:
Source: harava.news.

item.title: Yemen — no casualties reported in Friday's Aden attacks:
item.description:
AFP reports no casualties in Friday's ballistic-missile attacks on Aden's airport and Maashiq presidential palace, despite ambulances seen entering the palace compound; it remains unclear whether the missiles hit their targets.
The Houthis continue to deny the coalition's Mecca and Medina drone claims as fabrications. Source:

item.title: Mika — an open-source Android agent that runs apps on a hidden background screen:
item.description:
Mika (wangzan101/Mika, Apache-2.0) turns a tool-calling language model into a phone agent: type one sentence and it opens apps and websites, reads the screen, and taps, types and scrolls on a hidden second display while you keep using the phone.
Created October 29, it reached roughly 1,600–2,100 stars within two days and release v0.1.16 on October 31, with an MCP bridge so desktop agents can call it. Beta, and the README says so plainly — the privacy question is the whole story here, since handing a model your phone means handing it your apps.
Sources:
Source: explainx.ai.
item.content:encoded:
Mika (wangzan101/Mika, Apache-2.0) turns a tool-calling language model into a phone agent: type one sentence and it opens apps and websites, reads the screen, and taps, types and scrolls on a hidden second display while you keep using the phone.

Created October 29, it reached roughly 1,600–2,100 stars within two days and release v0.1.16 on October 31, with an MCP bridge so desktop agents can call it. Beta, and the README says so plainly — the privacy question is the whole story here, since handing a model your phone means handing it your apps.

item.title: Ivanti chain completed in KEV — patches now available, federal deadline Monday:
item.description:
CISA added two more Ivanti Connect Secure flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday, CVE-2026-111357 (CVSS 8.8, privilege escalation) and CVE-2026-118527 (CVSS 4.3, predictable identifiers enabling file upload), completing the three-flaw chain Volexity documented earlier this month: auth bypass CVE-2026-104935 plus these two give unauthenticated root-level code execution on a fully patched appliance, with the attacker observed extracting credentials and searching Active Directory for admin passwords and BitLocker keys.
Ivanti says fixes are available and its latest release addresses all three flaws; federal deadlines are November 2 for CVE-2026-111357 and November 13 for CVE-2026-118527. If you run Connect Secure, this is the patch.
Source:
Source: thehackernews.com.

item.title: US approves a $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine — but the missiles may not arrive until the 2030s
item.description:
The US State Department said on Friday it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, in what Reuters describes as one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration — and, in the same breath, a reminder of how slow the pipeline is: two people briefed on the decision told Reuters the missiles have yet to be manufactured and are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
The deal's shape matters as much as its size. According to Reuters, Ukraine will pay with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through the US JUMPSTART program, along with national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, and Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor. JUMPSTART uses allied donations to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine; Reuters notes it was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $825 million. In July, the US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce Patriot interceptors, with Lockheed saying that deal would let it triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030.
What each side says about the timing is where the tension sits. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, and he has repeatedly urged Washington to speed up deliveries ahead of winter. Reuters reports Ukraine's Defence Ministry is encouraging the Pentagon to bring the delivery date forward, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new interceptors. The US side has not publicly committed to that acceleration. The approval also lands against the other Friday friction covered in the evening brief: delayed deliveries have added to US-Ukraine tension after President Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for not stopping attacks on Russian refineries — attacks Ukraine resumed before dawn on Friday at Novokuibyshevsk.
For ordinary people in Ukraine, the gap between approval and arrival is the story. Patriot is the most effective weapon against fast-moving ballistic missiles, and Russia's campaign against the power grid is already the winter's defining threat — Thursday's drone strike on a crowded Dnipro rail platform killed at least 14 people, and five more died in daytime strikes on two other cities that day, according to officials cited by Reuters. A 500-missile order approved now but delivered in the 2030s does not keep the lights on this winter; what does, in the near term, is whatever interceptors allies can pull from existing stocks, which is exactly what Kyiv is now asking Washington to arrange.
In short: Friday's $2.1 billion approval is real and large, but it is a long-term order, not a winter delivery — and the thing to watch is whether the Pentagon agrees to hand over missiles from its own arsenal now and replace them later, because that is the only version of this deal that helps Ukraine before the 2030s.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Second holy-city drone claim in a day — Medina this time — as Houthi missiles hit Aden's airport and palace
item.description:
The Saudi-led coalition said on Friday evening it had intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by Yemen's Houthis over Saudi Arabia's Medina region, hours after the Mecca-region interception covered in the evening brief — and the Houthis denied both, calling the Medina claim a fabrication, on the same evening Yemeni government forces said Houthi ballistic missiles struck Aden's airport and the Maashiq presidential palace.
Reuters reports the coalition's Medina announcement came on Friday, with no statement of what the drone was aimed at or whether debris caused damage. Medina is home to one of Islam's holiest sites and is visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims each year, which is why the claim carries weight far beyond one drone. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree denied any operation directed at Saudi territory, saying in a social media post that the claim a drone was shot down over Medina was "merely a continuation of their grand and egregious fabrications." The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting Mecca and Medina, saying their operations target Saudi oil facilities and military bases, and that they publicly announce attacks when they occur. The coalition has now placed Houthi drones over the regions of both holy cities within a single day, according to a roundup of Friday's coalition statements, which also counted a cruise missile destroyed en route to western Saudi Arabia and a ballistic missile aimed at the southern region that day — four interceptions claimed in total, with the Houthis denying the holy-city claims.
The Aden side of Friday evening is reported by Yemen's government, not the coalition. Yemen Monitor reports that armed forces spokesman Colonel Majid Al-Nuzili said the Houthis targeted Aden International Airport and the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with ballistic missiles, in what he called a new attack on vital infrastructure in the temporary capital. Local residents reported two missiles launched from Ibb and Al-Dhalea governorates toward Aden, followed by three loud explosions across the city, and witnesses reported ambulances entering the palace compound. No casualty or damage figures had been made public by the early hours of Saturday. The Yemeni government called on the UN Security Council to take deterrent measures and enforce the arms embargo on the group. Aden airport had only resumed flights on Thursday morning after Wednesday evening's shelling forced a temporary suspension and emergency runway repairs.
For ordinary people, the two Friday threads hit different nerves. A drone claim over Medina, true or fabricated, lands on pilgrims and on Muslim public opinion worldwide — the Gulf Cooperation Council has previously called such strikes a violation of the sanctity of the holy sites — while Aden's airport is the south's humanitarian and civilian lifeline, already struck twice on October 28 and again on October 15, when the palace attack killed at least four people according to government officials. Each side is also using Friday's claims to frame the other: Riyadh presenting a pattern of holy-city targeting, the Houthis presenting a pattern of fabricated Saudi claims, and the Yemeni government presenting a pattern of attacks on civilian infrastructure that contradicts the Houthis' stated aim of ending the blockade on Yemen.
In short: Friday ended with the coalition claiming a drone downed over Medina and the Houthis denying it outright, while in Aden the government says missiles hit the airport and palace — claims and denials, no confirmed casualties yet, and two holy-city regions now named in coalition claims in a single day. Watch for any debris evidence, pilgrim-area impact, or casualty reporting that would settle whether Friday's Medina claim was a real interception or, as the Houthis insist, a fabrication.
Sources:
Source: yemenmonitor.com.

item.title: Ukraine hits a Russian refinery again — ending the US-pressed pause — as Oleshky evacuations finally begin
item.description:
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery before dawn on Friday for the first time since October 15, breaking a pause that the Wall Street Journal reports was held under sustained pressure from President Trump ahead of next Tuesday's US midterm elections — while, in the war's starkest contrast, residents of the Russian-held town of Oleshky began boarding evacuation buses on Friday under the local ceasefire both sides are still observing.
Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that builds the FP-1 drone, said its drones scored several hits across Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk refinery in the Samara region, including on a unit that hydrotreats diesel fuel. Footage posted by the monitoring channel Exilenova+ showed at least 11 separate fires on the site, and European Copernicus Sentinel satellite imagery published by Reuters showed smoke drifting from the refinery. Samara's governor, Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, confirmed only that air defences and mobile fire groups were working against a drone attack on the region, and flights at Samara's airport were delayed. The plant sits on the Volga about 1,000 km from Ukraine's border, can process about 8.3 million tonnes of crude a year, and makes jet fuel for the Russian Aerospace Forces — the air arm that drops glide bombs on Ukrainian cities, according to Reuters reporting cited by Yac News.
The Journal's account of the pause is the other half of the story. It reports that Ukrainian long-range units were told in mid-October that the refinery campaign was effectively on hold once missions already under way were complete, with the pause expected to last until after the November 3 midterms, possibly deeper into November. At a meeting in Oslo on October 20, Trump's envoy Jared Kushner pressed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for a 30-day pause as a way to show gratitude for US mediation, one US official told the Journal, describing the conversation as "very tough." European allies, the Journal reports, advised Zelenskyy to wait until after the vote to ease tension with Trump. Zelenskyy himself told reporters on October 27 that units had no order against hitting refineries and had simply tried "to be a little more careful during these days." Moscow's response on Friday was blunt: Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state television that Trump had been insistent about refinery strikes and that the Ukrainian government ignored him. "Once again they disobeyed," Ushakov said.
What each side says it wants in return has not changed, and that is why the pause broke. Zelenskyy told Trump, the Journal reports, that Ukraine would need something in return for halting refinery strikes: first choice a mutual energy ceasefire under which Russia would stop hitting Ukrainian power plants, alternatives Patriot missiles to protect the grid or permission to use Starlink inside Russia to destroy missile launchers. Ukraine received 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days against a need of about 350 a month, Zelenskyy said on October 26. Throughout the pause, Russian forces kept hitting Ukrainian power plants and cities — on Thursday a Russian jet-powered drone killed 15 people on a crowded platform at Dnipro's railway station — and the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry told the UN General Assembly on October 26 that Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy system followed a state policy of depriving civilians of electricity and amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity. Russia, for its part, still hopes Trump can pressure Kyiv into a deal meeting many of Moscow's conditions, including full Russian control of the Donbas and a bar on Ukraine joining NATO, while Kyiv wants US intelligence-sharing to continue and European-bought US hardware, including Patriot interceptors, to keep flowing.
For ordinary people, the two Friday developments pull in opposite directions. A refinery that fuels Russian warplanes is a military target with a civilian shadow: the same campaign has already cut Russian diesel output by about 30 percent by International Energy Agency estimates, feeding the fuel-price politics Trump cited when he announced a Russian diesel supply deal on October 9. In Oleshky, the human side is immediate and visible. Reuters reports that groups of residents began boarding evacuation buses on Friday — some heading to Russia, others to Ukraine — under the ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump with Pope Leo's involvement. Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi told parliament that residents headed for Ukraine would travel through Russia to Belarus before entering the Kyiv and Chernihiv regions, though he later retracted an early figure of 527 people planning to leave, saying no exact figures exist yet and the operation is ongoing. Newsmax's correspondent on the ground reported 750 people preregistered for evacuation from a town that had about 24,000 residents before the war and roughly 2,000 left. The ceasefire runs only until Sunday evening, and how many people actually get out before it expires is still unknown.
In short: the refinery pause lasted about two weeks, broke four days before the US midterms, and broke because Kyiv says it got no mutual energy ceasefire or air defences in return — while in Oleshky, the war's rarest thing, a ceasefire both sides are keeping, is now moving real people out of a town that has waited years for it. Watch whether Washington reacts to the Novokuibyshevsk strike, and whether the Oleshky buses keep rolling through the weekend.
Sources:
Source: yacnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery before dawn on Friday for the first time since October 15, breaking a pause that the Wall Street Journal reports was held under sustained pressure from President Trump ahead of next Tuesday's US midterm elections — while, in the war's starkest contrast, residents of the Russian-held town of Oleshky began boarding evacuation buses on Friday under the local ceasefire both sides are still observing.

Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that builds the FP-1 drone, said its drones scored several hits across Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk refinery in the Samara region, including on a unit that hydrotreats diesel fuel. Footage posted by the monitoring channel Exilenova+ showed at least 11 separate fires on the site, and European Copernicus Sentinel satellite imagery published by Reuters showed smoke drifting from the refinery. Samara's governor, Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, confirmed only that air defences and mobile fire groups were working against a drone attack on the region, and flights at Samara's airport were delayed. The plant sits on the Volga about 1,000 km from Ukraine's border, can process about 8.3 million tonnes of crude a year, and makes jet fuel for the Russian Aerospace Forces — the air arm that drops glide bombs on Ukrainian cities, according to Reuters reporting cited by Yac News.

The Journal's account of the pause is the other half of the story. It reports that Ukrainian long-range units were told in mid-October that the refinery campaign was effectively on hold once missions already under way were complete, with the pause expected to last until after the November 3 midterms, possibly deeper into November. Moscow's response on Friday was blunt: Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state television that Trump had been insistent about refinery strikes and that the Ukrainian government ignored him. "Once again they disobeyed," Ushakov said.

What each side says it wants in return has not changed, and that is why the pause broke. Zelenskyy told Trump, the Journal reports, that Ukraine would need something in return for halting refinery strikes: first choice a mutual energy ceasefire under which Russia would stop hitting Ukrainian power plants, alternatives Patriot missiles to protect the grid or permission to use Starlink inside Russia to destroy missile launchers. item.title: Iran claims three more tankers hit mines in Hormuz — unverified — as a Mecca drone claim is denied and Qatari mediators return to Tehran
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Friday that three oil tankers, including a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil, exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz — claims the US military disputes and the Associated Press could not verify — on the same day the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a Houthi drone near Mecca, a claim the Houthis flatly denied, and Qatari mediators returned to Tehran for talks.
The Guard's account, carried by Iranian state media, is that the tankers were using what Tehran calls unauthorised routes through the strait, had switched off their navigation systems, and ignored repeated radio warnings. Earlier on Friday the Guard's navy said two other tankers caught fire after striking mines, and later said a third — the supertanker — had done the same. No vessels were named and no crew details were given. The US military denies the mine claims, saying all internationally recognised primary transit routes through the waterway have been cleared of sea mines by US forces. Separately, Oman's Maritime Security Center said Oman evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker that was attacked 1.6 nautical miles off the Musandam coast and caught fire — but it is unclear whether that incident is the same as any of the three Iran described. That ambiguity matters: Thursday's verified limpet-mine attack on the tanker Louise 1, covered in the morning brief, was a different, confirmed incident, and Friday's claims must not be folded into it as if they were one event.
The Saudi claim and denial follow a pattern both sides have repeated for weeks. Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said a drone launched by the Houthis was intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region on Friday. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree denied it on X and Telegram, saying the group carried out no operation targeting Saudi territory on Friday at all, that its operations target Saudi oil facilities and military bases, and calling the Mecca claim a "gross and outrageous lie." The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities, and the coalition has repeatedly reported interceptions headed toward them. Neither side offered evidence on Friday beyond its own statement.
Diplomacy ran in parallel. Iranian state media said Qatari mediators, headed by the country's foreign minister and a senior adviser to the prime minister, returned to Tehran on Friday for talks with senior Iranian officials. The visit follows outreach from US Vice President JD Vance, who sent a letter in recent days to Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council; Tehran acknowledged receipt on Thursday but said it had not responded, and Trump suggested the letter was about possibly allowing humanitarian aid rather than peace negotiations. Diplomats say US officials have told Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections.
For ordinary people, the stakes are fuel prices, shipping safety, and, in Yemen itself, displacement. Brent crude had already pushed toward $117 on the week's tanker and refinery risk, as covered in the morning brief, and every new unverified claim moves that price before any damage is confirmed. In Yemen, the UN humanitarian office said the number of displaced people has passed 281,000 between August 1 and October 25, the overwhelming majority fleeing fighting in Taiz and along the west coast, with 263 civilian casualties documented including 67 killed — children accounting for 97 of the casualties and about half of those killed.
In short: Friday brought three Iranian tanker claims with no names, no crews and no independent verification, a disputed Mecca drone claim both sides are using to frame the other, and a fresh Qatari mediation visit — all against a US warning to allies to brace for possible post-midterms action. Treat the tanker claims as developing, not confirmed, and watch for a named vessel, a crew account, or satellite imagery that would settle them.
Sources:
Source: military.com.

item.title: Israel — coalition talks still waiting on formal certification:
item.description:
No mandate has been issued yet. The final results (Netanyahu bloc 53, Eisenkot bloc 48, Arab parties 19) were covered in the morning brief; Friday's coverage adds only pre-consultation manoeuvring.
All Israel News reports ultra-Orthodox party UTJ's leadership signalled it could enter talks with the Eisenkot-led Change Bloc, with an agreed IDF conscription law as its price — but a UTJ Knesset member's office denied to Channel 12 that party officials had been instructed to begin such talks. President Herzog is expected to begin consultations after the official results are submitted on November 4.
Sources:
Source: allisraelnews.com.

item.title: Ivanti's VPN chain is not finished — two more flaws hit CISA's exploited list Friday:
item.description:
CISA added CVE-2026-111357 (privilege escalation to root, CVSS 8.8 per Ivanti) and CVE-2026-118527 (predictable file location for uploads, CVSS 4.3) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 30.
Both are pieces of the same attack chain Volexity caught in early October, in which a group it calls UTA0576 broke into a fully patched Ivanti Connect Secure VPN without a password, got root, and went after Active Directory — LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys and service account credentials. Ivanti fixed the front door (CVE-2026-104935) on October 13, but the root step's patch only shipped on October 29: you need 22.8R2.6 or 25.1.1.3.
If you patched in mid-October and moved on, you are not done — and because the attackers cleaned up after themselves, a clean result from Ivanti's Integrity Checker does not prove the box was not hit. Federal deadlines: November 2 for CVE-2026-111357, November 13 for CVE-2026-118527.
Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: Binance to resume withdrawals within 48 hours after $6.3B hack — updated timeline:
item.description:
Friday's update narrows the morning brief's estimate: co-founder Yi He said withdrawals are now expected within about 42–45 hours as Binance rebuilds its withdrawal service and security environment, with deposits operating normally.
Binance says it has reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover the incident, $5 billion of it already held in the exact tokens affected, and will update its Proof of Reserves in the coming days. TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group — that attribution is from the research firm, not yet confirmed by Binance, which still describes "additional points of breach" beyond the initially reported compromised DevOps laptop.
About $3 billion remains frozen with industry partners. Sources:
Source: binance.com.

item.title: AU Small Finance Bank investigates suspected Salesforce data breach:
item.description:
AU Small Finance Bank said on October 30 it is investigating a potential data leak involving a Salesforce-managed SaaS platform holding limited data on its vehicle-loan customers.
The bank says its own systems remain unaffected and banking services are operating normally. A threat-intel post claims the Scarlett Group is behind it and lists KYC records, identity documents, financial records and loan agreements among the data types — that claim is unverified, and a person familiar with the matter told BusinessLine the KYC claims are "unverified and unvalidated."
Treat it as an investigation, not a confirmed breach. Source:

item.title: Russell Brand trial — prosecution closing Friday; jury still to retire:
item.description:
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones gave her closing speech at Southwark Crown Court on Friday, telling jurors six women who do not know one another independently came forward over a decade, that they were seeking closure after encounters that had "haunted them for years," and that Brand's behaviour changed from charming to threatening before he ignored objections — "He didn't listen when (they) said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care."
She used a stopwatch to hold 20 seconds of silence for the length of time one woman said she was pulled toward a workplace toilet in 2001. The judge has told jurors only a unanimous verdict will be accepted on each charge, and deliberations are expected to begin early next week, with Tuesday, November 3 the expected retirement date reported earlier.
Brand denies all seven charges (three rape, three sexual assault, one attempted indecent assault, six women, 1999–2009). Note: another low-quality blog post circulating Friday claims a verdict has already been returned; that contradicts AP/AAP court reporting showing the trial continuing on Friday, so it is not reported here as fact.
Sources:
Source: aapnews.aap.com.au.

item.title: Aid finally reaches Oleshky — while Russia hits Kyiv, Dnipro and Odesa overnight
item.description:
The war's strangest contrast played out overnight: in the Russian-held town of Oleshky, Ukrainian and Russian human-rights commissioners stood side by side as a long-awaited aid convoy arrived — while across the rest of Ukraine, Russia launched a massive overnight missile-and-drone strike on energy infrastructure, killing at least one person in Kyiv and leaving Dnipro's power system struggling after Thursday's deadly platform attack.
Reuters reports that residents of Oleshky were due to receive food and medical supplies on Friday and be allowed to leave if they wish, under a local ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump that has now held for more than three days. Russian commissioner Yana Lantratova and Ukrainian commissioner Dmytro Lubinets appeared together on Friday to update reporters. "The aid was assembled based on the specific needs reported to us; it includes food, hygiene products, essential medical supplies, fuel – everything the people require," Lantratova said. Lubinets said everyone in need would get help, including those who wished to leave — for Ukraine or for Russia. A fleet of 25 buses with room for 750 people, 50 medical personnel, ambulances for people with limited mobility, and even a bus with pet cages stood ready, according to Reuters and Lubinets' own account. The convoy had been assembled in Armiansk, about 85 km south of Oleshky, and departed Friday morning for the town's central hospital. The demining that made it possible cost lives: Lantratova said a sapper and one other person were killed during clearance operations.
At the same time, Ukraine's Air Force reported that from 6 p.m. Thursday, Russia attacked with Iskander-M and S-400 ballistic missiles, KN-23 missiles and four Kh-59/69 guided aviation missiles, plus 113 strike drones — 83 of them jet-powered. Air defences downed 99 targets, including 96 drones, but hits were recorded at 17 locations and debris fell at five more, according to Kyiv24 and 112.ua, citing the Air Force. The main directions were Kyiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk regions, but Prime Minister Serhiy Korytskyi said Kyiv, Chernihiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Poltava, Donetsk and Volyn regions were all under attack, with energy infrastructure the main target. In Kyiv, one person was killed and at least 12 residential buildings damaged across the capital, Kyiv region and Kharkiv region; four more people were injured in Kyiv, Donetsk, Kharkiv and Volyn. In Poltava, energy infrastructure and railway facilities were hit. Russia's Defence Ministry claimed a "massive" strike on drone-production and storage plants, the energy facilities powering them, and Odesa-region port infrastructure and vessels — claims that, as usual, came without named sites, numbers or imagery and could not be independently verified. Moscow also claimed it shot down 1,043 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, another unverified figure.
The two sides' framing of the wider war has not moved, even as they cooperated in Oleshky. Reuters notes Moscow still hopes President Trump can pressure Kyiv into accepting a deal meeting many of Russia's conditions, including full Russian control of the Donbas and a bar on Ukraine joining NATO. Kyiv, Reuters reports, wants US intelligence-sharing to continue, along with access to Elon Musk's recently disrupted Starshield battlefield communications system and continued flows of European-bought US hardware, including Patriot interceptors. On the next round of US-mediated talks, the picture clouded further: Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov linked the timing of the Abu Dhabi round to the Middle East conflict and the battlefield situation, according to Reuters via Zark News — putting Zelensky's hoped-for November 6–10 window in doubt, with Moscow still proposing no specific date. Earlier rounds have stalled over eastern-Ukrainian territory and security guarantees.
For ordinary people, the human ledger is stark. In Oleshky, a town seized in the first days of the 2022 invasion and badly flooded after the Kakhovka dam destruction in 2023, residents have described surviving on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, travelling mine-strewn roads — one known as the "road of death" — just for food and water, according to Reuters. Friday's convoy is the first relief of its kind in four years and eight months of war. In Dnipro, the toll from Thursday's railway-platform strike rose to 15 after a 40-year-old man died in hospital, and the city's mayor said Friday morning the power system could not withstand the attacks, urging residents to stay home as electric transport stopped running. The Oleshky ceasefire runs only until the evening of November 1, and evacuations onward — reportedly via Anapa in Russia to Gomel in Belarus on October 31 — are still to be confirmed by Kyiv.
In short: one town got its first aid in years because both sides agreed to stop shooting there for six days, while everywhere else the war escalated overnight — 113 drones and ballistic missiles at energy targets, one dead in Kyiv, Dnipro's grid buckling, and the next peace round drifting. Friday's convoy and Saturday's planned evacuations are the test of whether the Oleshky exception means anything beyond itself.
Sources:
Source: kyiv24.com.
item.content:encoded:
The war's strangest contrast played out overnight: in the Russian-held town of Oleshky, Ukrainian and Russian human-rights commissioners stood side by side as a long-awaited aid convoy arrived — while across the rest of Ukraine, Russia launched a massive overnight missile-and-drone strike on energy infrastructure, killing at least one person in Kyiv and leaving Dnipro's power system struggling after Thursday's deadly platform attack.

Reuters reports that residents of Oleshky were due to receive food and medical supplies on Friday and be allowed to leave if they wish, under a local ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump that has now held for more than three days. Russian commissioner Yana Lantratova and Ukrainian commissioner Dmytro Lubinets appeared together on Friday to update reporters. "The aid was assembled based on the specific needs reported to us; it includes food, hygiene products, essential medical supplies, fuel – everything the people require," Lantratova said. Lubinets said everyone in need would get help, including those who wished to leave — for Ukraine or for Russia. A fleet of 25 buses with room for 750 people, 50 medical personnel, ambulances for people with limited mobility, and even a bus with pet cages stood ready, according to Reuters and Lubinets' own account. The convoy had been assembled in Armiansk, about 85 km south of Oleshky, and departed Friday morning for the town's central hospital. The demining that made it possible cost lives: Lantratova said a sapper and one other person were killed during clearance operations.

At the same time, Ukraine's Air Force reported that from 6 p.m. Thursday, Russia attacked with Iskander-M and S-400 ballistic missiles, KN-23 missiles and four Kh-59/69 guided aviation missiles, plus 113 strike drones — 83 of them jet-powered. Air defences downed 99 targets, including 96 drones, but hits were recorded at 17 locations and debris fell at five more, according to Kyiv24 and 112.ua, citing the Air Force. The main directions were Kyiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk regions, but Prime Minister Serhiy Korytskyi said Kyiv, Chernihiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Poltava, Donetsk and Volyn regions were all under attack, with energy infrastructure the main target. In Kyiv, one person was killed and at least 12 residential buildings damaged across the capital, Kyiv region and Kharkiv region; four more people were injured in Kyiv, Donetsk, Kharkiv and Volyn. In Poltava, energy infrastructure and railway facilities were hit. Russia's Defence Ministry claimed a "massive" strike on drone-production and storage plants, the energy facilities powering them, and Odesa-region port infrastructure and vessels — claims that, as usual, came without named sites, numbers or imagery and could not be independently verified. Moscow also claimed it shot down 1,043 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, another unverified figure.

The two sides' framing of the wider war has not moved, even as they cooperated in Oleshky. Reuters notes Moscow still hopes President Trump can pressure Kyiv into accepting a deal meeting many of Russia's conditions, including full Russian control of the Donbas and a bar on Ukraine joining NATO. Kyiv, Reuters reports, wants US intelligence-sharing to continue, along with access to Elon Musk's recently disrupted Starshield battlefield communications system and continued flows of European-bought US hardware, including Patriot interceptors. On the next round of US-mediated talks, the picture clouded further: Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov linked the timing of the Abu Dhabi round to the Middle East conflict and the battlefield situation, according to Reuters via Zark News — putting Zelensky's hoped-for November 6–10 window in doubt, with Moscow still proposing no specific date. Earlier rounds have stalled over eastern-Ukrainian territory and security guarantees.

For ordinary people, the human ledger is stark. In Oleshky, a town seized in the first days of the 2022 invasion and badly flooded after the Kakhovka dam destruction in 2023, residents have described surviving on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, travelling mine-strewn roads — one known as the "road of death" — just for food and water, according to Reuters. Friday's convoy is the first relief of its kind in four years and eight months of war. In Dnipro, the toll from Thursday's railway-platform strike rose to 15 after a 40-year-old man died in hospital, and the city's mayor said Friday morning the power system could not withstand the attacks, urging residents to stay home as electric transport stopped running. The Oleshky ceasefire runs only until the evening of November 1, and evacuations onward — reportedly via Anapa in Russia to Gomel in Belarus on October 31 — are still to be confirmed by Kyiv.

In short: one town got its first aid in years because both sides agreed to stop shooting there for six days, while everywhere else the war escalated overnight — 113 drones and ballistic missiles at energy targets, one dead in Kyiv, Dnipro's grid buckling, and the next peace round drifting. Friday's convoy and Saturday's planned evacuations are the test of whether the Oleshky exception means anything beyond itself.

item.title: A new kind of tanker attack in Hormuz — limpet mines on a moving ship — as Houthi oil claims push Brent toward $117
item.description:
A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was hit by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat on Thursday night, in the first successful limpet-mine attack in the waterway since the US war with Iran began in February — and it landed on the same day Yemen's Houthis claimed strikes on Saudi Arabia's biggest refineries, sending Brent crude toward $117 a barrel.
Reuters, via gCaptain, reports that a small boat attached two limpet mines to the hull of the Panama-flagged tanker Louise 1, causing a fire in its engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel. The incident happened Thursday about 25 nautical miles northeast of Oman's Khasab, according to the British navy's United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which said the crew was safe, there was no environmental impact, the fire was extinguished and the vessel was continuing to its next port of call. Three maritime security sources identified the ship as the Louise 1; UKMTO itself did not name it. No one has been officially blamed. A September limpet-mine attempt in the area failed to detonate, two sources said, making this the first successful use of the method in this war. Greece-based maritime risk group Marisks warned that "the apparent ability of a small craft to approach a transiting tanker, deploy explosive devices and withdraw presents a significant security concern, particularly in the Strait's congested shipping lanes," calling the method "cheap, low tech and very efficient."
Iran's account differs. Iran's Army Navy claimed a tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait, and the IRGC claimed three — later four — tankers hit mines on an unauthorised southern route. UKMTO's verified account describes attached explosives, not a mine strike, and the two versions cannot both describe the same event in the same way. Separately, the Louise 1 has its own history: Reuters notes Ukrainian forces hit it in July with naval drones in the Black Sea over what Ukraine's SBU said was its role transporting Russian oil as part of the so-called shadow fleet.
The Hormuz attack came hours after the Houthi claims already covered in Thursday night's brief — six targets including Ras Tanura, Abqaiq and Rabigh refineries, Riyadh and Dammam airports and a Najran military headquarters — with the coalition confirming only two Riyadh intercepts. Friday's coverage adds no Saudi or Aramco confirmation of damage to any refinery, but Reuters' oil-market reporting confirms the market moved anyway: Brent rose 86 cents to $115.74 in early Friday trading and later hit $117, on track for a fourth monthly gain, with traders bracing for a possible post-midterms escalation in the US-Iran conflict.
For ordinary people, the stakes are fuel prices and shipping safety, not just geopolitics. Hormuz is the key sea outlet for Gulf crude, and a method that lets a small boat quietly attach explosives to a moving tanker in congested lanes is harder to defend against than a missile or drone that radar can see. The Louise 1 crew escaped unharmed and no oil spilled this time — but the incident, plus the unconfirmed refinery claims, is exactly the kind of supply-risk news that feeds through to petrol and diesel prices within weeks.
In short: nobody is officially blamed for the limpet-mine attack, Iran's mine story conflicts with UKMTO's attached-explosives account, and no refinery damage is confirmed — yet oil is up toward $117 on the risk alone. Watch for any Aramco statement, satellite imagery, or a second limpet incident, which would turn a one-off into a tactic.
Sources:
Source: gcaptain.com.

item.title: Israel — final results confirm the deadlock; Herzog's consultations are the next step:
item.description:
The Central Elections Committee released final results Friday morning: Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc 53 seats, Eisenkot's opposition bloc 48, Arab parties 19 — nobody near the 61 needed.
Official results go to President Isaac Herzog on November 4, the new Knesset is sworn in November 10, and Herzog is expected to begin consultations with party leaders as early as this weekend (Le Monde puts the start in the week of November 2). CNN's explainer lays out the four ways out: an opposition government, a Netanyahu-led deal (possibly via the ultra-Orthodox parties), a unity arrangement, or another election if nobody builds a majority within about 12 weeks.
The wrinkle to watch: if Arab parties formally recommend Eisenkot, he could present more recommendations than Netanyahu, forcing Herzog to choose between the largest single faction and the larger recommending bloc. Eisenkot met Naftali Bennett on Thursday evening to discuss forming a government "as quickly as possible."
Sources:
Source: ianslive.in.

item.title: Binance suffers what analysts call the biggest crypto heist ever — ~$6.3 billion impact, ~$3 billion frozen
item.description:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, said a security breach had an estimated $6.3 billion impact, which analysts said could amount to the biggest crypto heist on record — roughly four times the Bybit theft of 2025, according to Chainalysis, which put the amount actually stolen at $5.912 billion at the time of theft.
Reuters reports Binance worked with partners to freeze about $3 billion of affected assets so far, with no update on the remaining ~$3.3 billion. Co-founder Yi He said the company would cover "all hacking losses" from its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds, and Binance said user funds remain safe. The exchange temporarily suspended withdrawals (deposits continued normally, per later updates) and said it expects withdrawals to resume within about 45–48 hours. Tether froze nearly $1.57 billion, Circle more than $800 million, Ripple roughly $200 million, and World Liberty Financial froze funds with custodian BitGo.
What happened is still developing, and Binance's own account shifted during Friday. Its initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, which let an attacker access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions. By Friday morning, Binance said investigators had uncovered "additional points of breach," and co-CEO Richard Teng said the attacker "did not simply use one engineer's permissions" — so the laptop story is not the whole attack. Binance said it found no evidence of wallet private-key leaks, and analysts suspect North Korea's TraderTraitor operation, though that attribution is unconfirmed. Bitcoin fell to a six-week low around $76,470, down about 3%, with ether down more than 3%.
For ordinary people: if you hold crypto on Binance, withdrawals are paused while the exchange rebuilds its withdrawal service — Binance says user funds are covered, but expect delays and a detailed post-mortem, not instant clarity. The bigger lesson is the one analysts flagged: a single compromised employee laptop apparently opened a path to billions, which is why the "additional breach points" finding matters more than the first explanation.
Sources:
Source: bworldonline.com.

item.title: TeamViewer patches three high-severity flaws — update to 15.83:
item.description:
CVE-2026-111585 (CVSS 8.8, integer overflow in remote-control screen processing) and CVE-2026-92372 (CVSS 8.8, out-of-bounds write in the screen-image decoder) could let a malicious or compromised host execute code on the support technician's (viewer's) machine — the attack runs the wrong way round from the usual remote-access threat.
CVE-2026-92374 (7.8, macOS) is a local privilege-escalation via a TOCTOU/symlink flaw in the privileged helper. TeamViewer says it was not aware of any of these being exploited in the wild when it published bulletin TV-2026-1011 on October 27.
If you use TeamViewer to support others, patch before connecting to untrusted hosts. Source:
Source: securityweek.com.

item.title: Drupal Commerce Core flaw actively exploited — update and audit orders:
item.description:
CVE-2026-118539, a "highly critical" (21/25 on Drupal's scale) missing-authorisation flaw in Commerce Core, is being actively exploited in the wild, Drupal warned.
Unauthenticated attackers can bypass protections on certain routes and entity fields, with possible financial impact for store owners. Fix: Commerce Core 3.3.13 (3.x) or 8.x-2.41 (2.x) — updating Drupal core alone does not fix it — then audit orders for inconsistencies.
The module is used on 42,000+ sites. Drupal has not said how many sites were hit or whether it was exploited as a zero-day.
Source:
Source: thehackernews.com.
