item.title: Russell Brand trial — closing arguments and judge's directions Friday; deliberations expected Tuesday:
item.description:
The defence case concluded Thursday — Brand's barrister Polly Dyer closed by telling jurors Brand has no convictions other than a 1995 cannabis-possession fine — and on Friday the judge gave jurors step-by-step directions on the law they must follow for each charge, after prosecution closing arguments.
Brand denies all seven charges (three rape, three sexual assault, one attempted indecent assault, six women, 1999–2009). Multiple reports say the jury is expected to retire to consider verdicts on Tuesday, November 3.
Note: one low-quality search result circulating Friday claimed a verdict had already been returned; that contradicts the court reporting showing directions being given Friday and deliberations expected Tuesday, so it is not reported here as fact. Sources:
Source: britbrief.co.uk.

item.title: Night falls, strikes continue: Kyiv hit by ballistic missiles, 350,000 in Dnipro left without power — while Oleshky's aid delivery is set for Friday
item.description:
Hours after Thursday's deadly daytime strikes, Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles late Thursday night and knocked out power for around 350,000 people in and around Dnipro — even as both sides' envoys headed toward Oleshky, where the first aid delivery under the local truce is expected Friday.
Reuters reports that Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles late Thursday, hitting warehouses on the east side of the Dnipro River and starting a fire, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko, with Reuters witnesses reporting explosions in the city. The Kyiv Independent, via its overnight report, puts the toll at one person killed in Kyiv, with warehouse buildings in the Darnytskyi district struck just after 10 p.m. local time. In Dnipro, strikes on energy infrastructure left at least 350,000 people without power, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha, and another strike hit a student dormitory and set it ablaze. CNN adds a further Thursday detail: an employee of the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant was killed by a drone, an attack the International Atomic Energy Agency condemned.
The two sides' framing has not moved. President Volodymyr Zelensky called Thursday's daytime strikes "deliberate strikes against civilians, brazen in their cruelty," carried out "right as the humanitarian operation in Oleshky is unfolding," and warned Ukraine had intelligence about preparations for new ballistic missile strikes — a warning borne out hours later in Kyiv. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "heartbroken" by the "senseless and indiscriminate" Dnipro attack and urged allies to mount pressure on Russia. Moscow, which has consistently denied deliberately targeting civilians, had made no public comment on the Dnipro strike in early reporting, and has made clear the Oleshky truce applies only to the Kherson region, not the wider war. Zelensky also said Russia has launched over 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since October 14, and said in his nightly address that Ukraine had struck two Russian fighter-bomber planes and an Iskander launcher — a claim Moscow had not commented on.
For ordinary people, the night's strikes are the winter-war pattern in miniature: a capital of around three million under repeated ballistic-missile fire, and a major city, Dnipro, losing power for hundreds of thousands of households on the same day 14 people were killed on its railway platform. The Oleshky exception is the counterpoint. The six-day truce there, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump with Pope Leo's involvement, has now held for 54 hours without a reported violation, according to Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets. Both ombudsmen — Lantratova for Russia, Lubinets for Ukraine — said Thursday that demining was complete and the convoy was ready, heading first for the district hospital. Reuters reports Lantratova travelled into Oleshky on Thursday with four Newsmax journalists, while Lubinets led a Ukrainian delegation to the area. Ukrainian officials expect aid delivery on Friday, October 30, with evacuations of residents who wish to leave reportedly planned for Saturday, October 31 — via Anapa in Russia and then Gomel in Belarus, according to documents reported by Fox News and Ukraine's ombudsman office, a route Kyiv has neither confirmed nor denied, chosen, the office said, because the front-line approach is mined and there is no river crossing.
In short: Thursday's toll across Ukraine rose to at least 20 — 14 on the Dnipro platform, five in daytime strikes in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk, and one in the late-night Kyiv missile attack — while the Oleshky truce held into its third day and its convoy is due to move Friday. The truce runs only until 10:59 p.m. local time on November 1, so Friday's delivery is the test of whether it is real.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

CNN adds a further Thursday detail: an employee of the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant was killed by a drone, an attack the International Atomic Energy Agency condemned.

President Volodymyr Zelensky called Thursday's daytime strikes "deliberate strikes against civilians, brazen in their cruelty," carried out "right as the humanitarian operation in Oleshky is unfolding," and warned Ukraine had intelligence about preparations for new ballistic missile strikes — a warning borne out hours later in Kyiv. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "heartbroken" by the "senseless and indiscriminate" Dnipro attack and urged allies to mount pressure on Russia. Moscow, which has consistently denied deliberately targeting civilians, had made no public comment on the Dnipro strike in early reporting, and has made clear the Oleshky truce applies only to the Kherson region, not the wider war. Zelensky also said Russia has launched over 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since October 14, and said in his nightly address that Ukraine had struck two Russian fighter-bomber planes and an Iskander launcher — a claim Moscow had not commented on.

For ordinary people, the night's strikes are the winter-war pattern in miniature: a capital of around three million under repeated ballistic-missile fire, and a major city, Dnipro, losing power for hundreds of thousands of households on the same day 14 people were killed on its railway platform. The Oleshky exception is the counterpoint. The six-day truce there, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump with Pope Leo's involvement, has now held for 54 hours without a reported violation, according to Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets. Both ombudsmen — Lantratova for Russia, Lubinets for Ukraine — said Thursday that demining was complete and the convoy was ready, heading first for the district hospital. Reuters reports Lantratova travelled into Oleshky on Thursday with four Newsmax journalists, while Lubinets led a Ukrainian delegation to the area. Ukrainian officials expect aid delivery on Friday, October 30, with evacuations of residents who wish to leave reportedly planned for Saturday, October 31 — via Anapa in Russia and then Gomel in Belarus, according to documents reported by Fox News and Ukraine's ombudsman office, a route Kyiv has neither confirmed nor denied, chosen, the office said, because the front-line approach is mined and there is no river crossing.

In short: Thursday's toll across Ukraine rose to at least 20 — 14 on the Dnipro platform, five in daytime strikes in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk, and one in the late-night Kyiv missile attack — while the Oleshky truce held into its third day and its convoy is due to move Friday. The truce runs only until 10:59 p.m. local time on November 1, so Friday's delivery is the test of whether it is real.

Sources:

Source: reuters.com — Read the full article

item.title: Houthis claim six strikes across Saudi Arabia — refineries, both main airports, a military HQ — but Riyadh confirms only two Riyadh intercepts
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis claimed a six-target wave across Saudi Arabia on Thursday evening — three oil facilities, both of the kingdom's main commercial airports, and a military command headquarters — but the Saudi-led coalition confirmed only two ballistic missiles intercepted over Riyadh, leaving the other five claims unverified.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree named Ras Tanura refinery, Aramco's Abqaiq processing facility, the Rabigh refinery on the Red Sea coast, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, and a Saudi military headquarters in the Najran region, according to Al Jazeera and Middle East Eye as carried by the House of Saud, with Xinhua carrying the same six-target claim. Saree framed the wave as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Houthi-held areas, saying operations would continue "until Saudi acts of aggression cease and the blockade is lifted." Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki confirmed air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh — the sole Saudi confirmation from any of the six claimed targets — and Saudi Civil Defence said shrapnel from the interception wounded one citizen and damaged one house and one vehicle. No Saudi, coalition or Aramco statement has addressed the other five targets, including Saree's claims of disrupted air traffic at Dammam and of deaths and wounded at the Najran headquarters.
The gap between claim and confirmation is the pattern of this month, not an exception: on October 24 the Houthis claimed eight targets and the coalition confirmed two intercepts. What is new in this wave is Abqaiq, not publicly claimed as a Houthi target in 2026 before Thursday — the facility whose September 2019 attack temporarily removed roughly 5% of global daily oil supply. The wave also landed hours after flydubai extended its Saudi suspension to November 1, scrapping a plan to resume Riyadh and Dammam flights on October 30 — the two airports Saree named. No airline statement directly links the extension to the six-target announcement.
For ordinary people, the practical effects are already visible even without confirmation of the refinery claims: Saudi air travel remains disrupted, with Emirates set for Jeddah on October 30 but Riyadh and Dammam not until November 8 and Etihad suspended until at least November 5, and the threat alone keeps airlines away. Inside Yemen, the exchange continues in both directions and both sides' tallies are unverified: Yemen's government forces claimed 749 strikes on Houthi positions in 24 hours, neutralising 239 fighters, while the Houthis claimed 101 Saudi-led strikes across Sanaa and eight provinces, and earlier Thursday accused coalition strikes of killing 14 people at an Al-Jawf market and fuel station. The Institute for the Study of War separately notes the Yemeni government accused the Houthis of using chemical weapons in Taiz on October 28 — a claim it says came with no evidence and no local corroboration. The six-target wave also came three days after Saudi Arabia, Iran, Turkey and Pakistan issued a joint communiqué after talks in Tehran on October 26; the Houthis were not party to that meeting.
In short: six targets claimed, two Riyadh intercepts confirmed, one person wounded by shrapnel — and no confirmation yet for Abqaiq, Ras Tanura, Rabigh, Dammam airport or the Najran headquarters. Until Aramco, aviation authorities or satellite imagery weigh in, this is a claim about reach, not a confirmed hit on Saudi oil infrastructure. Developing.
Sources:
Source: houseofsaud.com.

item.title: Israel — deadlock, with a timetable and a fraud allegation:
item.description:
No bloc has the 61 seats needed to govern (Likud bloc 53, opposition 48, Arab parties 19).
President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party leaders on Friday; official final results are due November 4, triggering a November 11 deadline for Herzog to name who tries first to form a government, with about 100 days for the whole process before another election becomes unavoidable. On Thursday, Netanyahu alleged without evidence that the Arab parties' record gains were driven partly by voter fraud — a charge Arab leaders rejected as incitement — and Qatar denied interfering in the election after Israeli officials and media accused Arab parties of receiving Qatari funds.
Sources:
Source: 1027wbow.com.

item.title: Nvidia's $12.93B Hugging Face deal draws reported DOJ questions:
item.description:
Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported October 28 that Justice Department officials have asked how Nvidia's proposed Hugging Face purchase could affect AI competition.
Nvidia declined to comment, Hugging Face did not respond, and DOJ declined to discuss matters before the department. An inquiry is not a finding of wrongdoing, and the report does not establish the deal will be blocked.
The deal, announced September 3, is expected to close in the first half of 2027 if approved. Separately, Reuters reported Thursday night (citing The Information) that Nvidia is in talks to offer credit guarantees for AI cloud provider Nscale's debt funding for a West Virginia data centre Anthropic plans to use — unconfirmed, terms could change, and Nvidia, Nscale and Anthropic did not immediately respond to Reuters.
Sources:
Source: pcgeek.info.

item.title: CISA adds GitLab's CVSS 10.0 flaw to KEV — and patching GitLab alone may not fix it:
item.description:
CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow in how GitLab compiles regular expressions in CI/CD configs, allows unauthenticated remote code execution; the bug sits in Onigmo, the regex engine in Ruby.
CISA added it October 29 with a federal deadline of November 1. Alpine Linux disclosed October 28 that its own server was probed October 20–21, crashing workers eight times, after it had upgraded to 19.3.4 instead of the fixed 19.3.5 — and that upgrading to 19.3.6 still left it vulnerable, because GitLab's fix is a patch to the Ruby bundled in its own Linux packages and container images, not in GitLab's code alone.
Check your install type, not just your GitLab version. Source:
Source: pbxscience.com.

item.title: A deadly day on Ukraine's railways — and the Oleshky aid convoy is finally ready to roll
item.description:
A Russian drone strike on a crowded railway platform in Dnipro killed at least 14 people on Thursday, in one of the deadliest single strikes on Ukrainian passenger rail this year — on the same day Russia and Ukraine jointly announced that demining around the besieged town of Oleshky is complete and its long-awaited humanitarian convoy is ready to depart.
Reuters reports that a jet-powered drone hit a platform at Dnipro's main station while a commuter train was preparing to leave for Zaporizhzhia, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 more, including an 11-year-old boy, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha and state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia. Five more people were killed in daytime strikes elsewhere: two teenagers on a central street in Chernihiv, where 23 more were wounded, and three people in a strike on an apartment building in Kremenchuk, where 15 were wounded. An elevated threat level had been announced ahead of the Dnipro strike, Ukrzaliznytsia chief Oleksandr Pertsovsky said — but, he added, "unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform."
The two sides framed the day in opposite terms. Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said on Telegram that "Russia is deliberately hunting civilians: on trains, at stations, in residential buildings," and President Volodymyr Zelensky urged the US, Europe and the G7 to tighten sanctions, pointedly asking how many strikes Russia has carried out since sanctions were lifted on Russian oligarchs and the energy sector. Moscow, which has consistently denied deliberately targeting civilians, made no public comment on the Dnipro strike in early reporting — but it did make clear the six-day humanitarian truce applies only to the Kherson region, not the wider war. Meanwhile, in a rare joint statement, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday that "demining operations of routes have been completed for the humanitarian mission in Oleshky" and "the humanitarian convoy is ready for departure," heading first for the district hospital, with aid packages to follow and residents wishing to leave permitted to go within a set time frame.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the contrast is the war in miniature: commuters on an ordinary Dnipro–Zaporizhzhia train — a route carrying workers, families and students daily — caught in a strike on civilian rail, while in Oleshky, a town of mostly elderly residents that has endured months of shelling and shortages of food and medicine, a six-day window running to November 1 may finally bring relief. The catch, noted in Thursday coverage, is that ruined Dnieper bridges mean most Oleshky evacuees cannot reach Ukrainian-held territory directly, with Kremlin-appointed authorities proposing travel via Crimea — a route with legal and humanitarian complications of its own.
In short: at least 19 people were killed across Ukraine on Thursday, most of them on a Dnipro rail platform, even as the Oleshky truce held into its third day and its aid convoy was declared ready — the test now is whether the trucks actually move and civilians actually get out on Friday. Diplomats have also discussed a possible three-way Ukraine–Russia–US meeting in Abu Dhabi between November 6 and 10, though the Kremlin has cast doubt on that timetable.
Sources:
Source: northlandnewsradio.com.

item.title: Hormuz: a fourth tanker claimed ablaze, a burning ship confirmed near Oman — and the US denies Iran captured its drone
item.description:
Iran's mine claims in the Strait of Hormuz escalated again on Thursday, with Tehran now saying a fourth tanker is ablaze — while the one independently confirmed fact remains a single burning vessel near Oman, and Washington publicly denied a separate Iranian claim that it had captured an American drone.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said Thursday that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire over the past 24 hours after striking sea mines while using what Tehran calls an unauthorized southern route through the strait, according to Iranian state media carried by Arab News, Saudi Gazette and Xinhua. The IRGC said the vessels had switched off radar and navigation systems, ignored its warnings, and were abandoned along the strait's southern coast — but, as with every mine claim this month, it named no ships, flags, operators or casualties. Later Thursday, News18 reported a fourth tanker ablaze after a mine strike, again without independent confirmation. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre confirmed in Warning 185-26 that a vessel was burning about 9 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at around 0300 UTC — but identified neither the cause nor the crew's condition, and no connection between that sighting and the IRGC's claimed tankers has been established. A commercial consultancy, Vanguard Tech, assessed the vessel had been hit by a projectile and was mostly submerged, but that assessment has not been corroborated by any government agency.
Washington disputes the mine story outright. US Central Command's standing position is that all internationally recognized primary transit routes through Hormuz have been cleared of mines by US forces and remain so — while the IRGC told shipowners not to "pay attention to the illusions of the U.S. Central Command on social media." The two accounts can't both be right about the southern lane, which CENTCOM has been directing commercial vessels to use and the IRGC calls unauthorized and mined. The International Maritime Organization warned on October 27 that the Hormuz traffic route has mines and it cannot guarantee safe transit. And in a separate denial, CENTCOM called false Iran's claim that its electronic warfare unit had captured a US MQM-170 surveillance drone west of the strait.
For ordinary people, the dispute is priced into every fill-up: Brent crude was trading in the $114–$117 range on October 27–28, war-risk insurance for a single Hormuz transit has reached 6–10% of hull value (up from about 0.25% before the conflict), and ship-tracking data showed only about 25 strait crossings in the 24 hours to midday Thursday, with roughly 0.48 million barrels moving outbound — about 96% below pre-war levels. OPEC+ meets November 1, three days from now, with Saudi Arabia's quota set at 10.5 million barrels per day against actual export capacity constrained by the strait.
In short: Iran claims four tankers hit mines — unverified, unnamed, and disputed by CENTCOM — while one burning vessel near Oman is confirmed without a cause, and a US drone-capture claim was denied. Developing: vessel names, flags and crew outcomes are the facts to watch.
Sources:
Source: houseofsaud.com.

The IRGC said the vessels had switched off radar and navigation systems, ignored its warnings, and were abandoned along the strait's southern coast — but, as with every mine claim this month, it named no ships, flags, operators or casualties. Later Thursday, News18 reported a fourth tanker ablaze after a mine strike, again without independent confirmation. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre confirmed in Warning 185-26 that a vessel was burning about 9 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at around 0300 UTC — but identified neither the cause nor the crew's condition, and no connection between that sighting and the IRGC's claimed tankers has been established. A commercial consultancy, Vanguard Tech, assessed the vessel had been hit by a projectile and was mostly submerged, but that assessment has not been corroborated by any government agency.

Washington disputes the mine story outright. US Central Command's standing position is that all internationally recognized primary transit routes through Hormuz have been cleared of mines by US forces and remain so — while the IRGC told shipowners not to "pay attention to the illusions of the U.S. Central Command on social media." The two accounts can't both be right about the southern lane, which CENTCOM has been directing commercial vessels to use and the IRGC calls unauthorized and mined. The International Maritime Organization warned on October 27 that the Hormuz traffic route has mines and it cannot guarantee safe transit. And in a separate denial, CENTCOM called false Iran's claim that its electronic warfare unit had captured a US MQM-170 surveillance drone west of the strait.

For ordinary people, the dispute is priced into every fill-up: Brent crude was trading in the $114–$117 range on October 27–28, war-risk insurance for a single Hormuz transit has reached 6–10% of hull value (up from about 0.25% before the conflict), and ship-tracking data showed only about 25 strait crossings in the 24 hours to midday Thursday, with roughly 0.48 million barrels moving outbound — about 96% below pre-war levels. OPEC+ meets November 1, three days from now, with Saudi Arabia's quota set at 10.5 million barrels per day against actual export capacity constrained by the strait.

In short: Iran claims four tankers hit mines — unverified, unnamed, and disputed by CENTCOM — while one burning vessel near Oman is confirmed without a cause, and a US drone-capture claim was denied. Developing: vessel names, flags and crew outcomes are the facts to watch.

item.title: Israel — final count confirmed, still no government:
item.description:
Israel's Central Elections Committee finished counting every ballot Thursday, including double-envelope votes from soldiers and diplomats.
The final breakdown stands at 53 seats for Netanyahu's bloc, 48 for the opposition bloc, and 19 for the Arab parties — with Likud the largest single party at 27 seats (one more than the 26 in near-final morning figures), followed by Eisenkot's Yashar at 21 and Bennett's B'Yachad at 12. Nobody has the 61 needed to govern; President Isaac Herzog must now decide who tries first to form a coalition, with official final figures due next week.
Sources:
Source: unitedwithisrael.org.

item.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon — its new top-ranked AI model, built for cybersecurity, and almost nobody can use it yet
item.description:
Google unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon on Wednesday, its second frontier model in two weeks, positioning it as the company's strongest model yet for cybersecurity work — finding vulnerabilities, validating whether they can be exploited, and patching them at the root cause — but access is deliberately restricted to a small group of cyber defenders for now.
Reuters reports that Carbon follows Gemini 4 Argon, introduced two weeks earlier, and is being made available first to a subset of cybersecurity defenders through Google's Fairwind Program as the company continues testing safeguards, including participation in the US government's voluntary pre-release model testing. Google says Carbon ranks first on version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 59, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra on that ranking, and reports 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability discovery, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploit development, and 71% on CWE-bench for software patching. It also says Carbon generates secure code at more than twice Argon's success rate on internal benchmarks, and that internal teams watched it sustain hard engineering tasks over multiple days. Introductory API pricing matches Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising to $4/$20 after the introductory period.
The other side of the story is caution. Those benchmark figures are Google's own, not independent tests, and outside evaluation will matter once more people can actually run the model — one analysis notes the Intelligence Index lead over Opus 5.5 is a single point, and that Carbon's hallucination rate rose from Argon's. Google itself gives no date for wider developer, business or consumer availability, saying only "as soon as possible" while it gathers feedback and iterates on guardrails. The restricted rollout is the point: a model this good at finding and exploiting flaws is dual-use by nature, useful to defenders patching software and to attackers hunting the same bugs.
For ordinary people, Carbon matters indirectly but concretely: it is aimed at the defenders who patch the software everything else runs on, and its first users are the security teams at banks, hospitals, utilities and government agencies. If it works as claimed, vulnerabilities get found and fixed faster; if its guardrails fail, the same capability is in the wild. Either way, most users won't touch it directly for a while — the Gemini app and general developer access come later, undated.
In short: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon tops the Artificial Analysis index and posts striking self-reported security benchmarks, but it ships first only to vetted cyber defenders through Fairwind, with wider access undated — a deliberately slow rollout for a deliberately powerful tool.
Sources:
Source: dukecountry.fm.

item.title: CISA adds exploited Cisco ASA/FTD VPN crash flaw to KEV:
item.description:
CVE-2026-76418 (CVSS 8.6) lets an unauthenticated remote attacker crash Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD devices via the Remote Access SSL VPN service when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group.
Cisco's PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October 2026; CISA's federal deadline is November 1. Mitigation: disable secondary authentication on tunnel groups or disable the tunnel group list — there are no workarounds.

item.title: Russell Brand trial — judge halts wife's evidence, jury excused until Friday:
item.description:
After Laura Brand's character testimony on Thursday — calling her husband "caring," "kind" and "an amazingly attentive husband" — the judge intervened during defence questioning ("no, no, no") and Laura Brand was escorted from Southwark Crown Court; the jury was excused until Friday morning.
A former girlfriend, Elia Alvarez Diaz, also gave a statement describing Brand as "gentle" and "loving," saying "when I said no, however, he accepted it," and that their 1998–99 relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly. Brand denies all seven charges (three rape, three sexual assault, one attempted indecent assault, six women, 1999–2009).

item.title: Ukraine's biggest drone wave yet hits toward Moscow as Russia strikes Kharkiv — and a fragile truce holds in the south
item.description:
Overnight, Ukraine sent one of the largest drone waves of the war toward the Russian capital, while Russia kept hitting Ukrainian cities — and in the south, a rare US-brokered truce is holding just long enough for an aid mission to move.
Reuters reports that Russia downed most of 613 drones heading toward Moscow overnight, according to Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin, who reported the figure on Telegram. In Ukraine, Russia attacked Kharkiv, the country's second-biggest city, damaging an educational institution, mayor Ihor Terekhov said. Times Now's overnight coverage adds that the Kharkiv strikes hit at least two districts — Saltivskyi, where the educational institution was struck, and Kholodnohirskyi, where a separate attack sparked a fire — and that Russian forces used both jet-powered and conventional attack drones. The scale of the Moscow-bound wave stands out: it follows a week in which Ukrainian officials tallied 787 Russian drones and 26 civilians killed, and it comes days after Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian energy targets.
The two sides tell the story very differently. Moscow frames its air defenses as having blunted the attack, with Sobyanin's account emphasizing how many drones were downed; Kyiv's account, via Terekhov, emphasizes the civilian infrastructure hit in Kharkiv. Neither side's overnight claims have been independently verified, and casualty figures from Kharkiv were not yet confirmed in early reporting.
Meanwhile, the war's other overnight story is a truce that is actually holding. Reuters reports that neither Ukraine nor Russia has reported any violations so far of the US-brokered six-day ceasefire that took effect early Tuesday around the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, to allow evacuations and aid deliveries. Russia's human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova was en route to Oleshky on Thursday with four journalists from the US outlet Newsmax, while her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets was also heading to the area. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, via Interfax, that demining is under way and that Moscow hopes residents will be able to receive aid "today or tomorrow" and that those wishing to leave will be able to do so. The truce was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump with the involvement of Pope Leo, and applies to the town and surrounding areas, including the wider Kherson region, which has suffered years of near-daily drone and artillery attacks. Residents there have faced regular shelling and severe shortages of food and medicine, with Moscow and Kyiv blaming each other for the situation — which is why the mission matters more than the headlines: if aid actually gets in Thursday or Friday, it will be the first relief for people trapped in the town in months.
For ordinary people, the night captures the war's split reality: in Moscow and Kharkiv, air-raid routines and damaged schools; in Oleshky, a six-day window — running to November 1 — in which civilians may finally get food, medicine, or a way out. What to watch: whether the Oleshky evacuations actually begin Friday as planned, and whether the record-size Moscow drone wave draws a Russian retaliation barrage.
In short: Ukraine launched a record-scale drone wave at Moscow, Russia hit Kharkiv, and a rare truce around Oleshky is holding — with an aid mission expected Thursday or Friday.
Sources:
Source: 985theriver.com.

item.title: Iran claims three tankers hit mines in Hormuz as US warns allies of post-midterm strikes — and a back-channel letter surfaces
item.description:
The Strait of Hormuz standoff sharpened overnight on two fronts at once: a disputed claim of new tanker sinkings, and fresh signs Washington is preparing allies — and Tehran — for what comes after next Tuesday's US midterms.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said Thursday that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking sea mines while using what Tehran calls an unauthorized southern route through the Strait of Hormuz over the past 24 hours, according to Iranian state media carried by Reuters and others. The IRGC said the vessels had switched off their radar and navigation systems, ignored its warnings, and were abandoned along the strait's southern coast. It did not name the ships, their flags, or their crews. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) confirmed a vessel burning about 9 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at around 0300 UTC — but identified neither the cause nor the crew's condition, and no connection between that sighting and the three tankers has been established.
Washington disputes the mine story outright. US Central Command said earlier this week that Iranian mine claims are "false," that US forces have cleared the internationally recognized main transit routes, and that thousands of vessels are passing safely. IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi challenged Washington on Thursday to provide independent evidence for its mine-clearance claims. The two accounts can't both be right about the main shipping lanes — and the gap between them is exactly what keeps war-risk insurance premiums at record levels and many tankers rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope.
At the same time, the diplomatic track is moving in parallel with the military one. Two diplomats briefed on US warnings told reporters that Washington has urged Middle East allies to prepare for possible renewed strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterms, with a campaign that could last several days, and to brace for Iranian retaliation against energy facilities. Separately, the Wall Street Journal first reported — via Axios and other outlets — that Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, saying any talks to avert a US strike must address Iran's nuclear program. It is described as the highest-level US contact with Tehran in months. President Trump publicly offered a different explanation on Wednesday, saying the letter was about getting medical supplies into Iran. Tehran, for its part, wants the US naval blockade lifted, frozen money released, and oil sales cleared before further engagement — while Washington insists nuclear talks come first and sanctions relief follows progress. Iran's foreign minister said Thursday that Tehran is still giving diplomacy a chance under a seven-day stepwise de-escalation plan, while Iranian security officials warned of broader retaliation if attacked. Iran also dismissed a Qatari peace draft as "unacceptable ideas," according to Thursday analysis.
For ordinary people, the stakes are the gas pump and the grocery bill: Brent crude slipped to about $114.10 a barrel and WTI to about $101.45 in early Thursday trading as diplomacy headlines briefly outweighed the tanker claims — still far above pre-crisis levels, and still hostage to whether the strait stays open. OPEC+ meets November 1, three days from now.
In short: Iran claims three tankers hit mines in Hormuz — unverified and disputed by CENTCOM — while the US warns allies to prepare for possible post-midterm strikes and a Vance letter tests whether nuclear talks can head them off. Developing.
Sources:
Source: en.hathalyoum.net.

Tehran, for its part, wants the US naval blockade lifted, frozen money released, and oil sales cleared before further engagement — while Washington insists nuclear talks come first and sanctions relief follows progress. Iran's foreign minister said Thursday that Tehran is still giving diplomacy a chance under a seven-day stepwise de-escalation plan, while Iranian security officials warned of broader retaliation if attacked. Iran also dismissed a Qatari peace draft as "unacceptable ideas," according to Thursday analysis.

For ordinary people, the stakes are the gas pump and the grocery bill: Brent crude slipped to about $114.10 a barrel and WTI to about $101.45 in early Thursday trading as diplomacy headlines briefly outweighed the tanker claims — still far above pre-crisis levels, and still hostage to whether the strait stays open. OPEC+ meets November 1, three days from now.

In short: Iran claims three tankers hit mines in Hormuz — unverified and disputed by CENTCOM — while the US warns allies to prepare for possible post-midterm strikes and a Vance letter tests whether nuclear talks can head them off. Developing.

item.title: Yemen: 749 government strikes in 24 hours, 101 Saudi strikes claimed, and 14 reported killed at a market
item.description:
Fighting inside Yemen surged to a new intensity overnight, even as Houthi missiles kept flying at Saudi territory.
Government forces said they carried out 749 attacks on Houthi command centres, fortifications, vehicles and supply lines over the past 24 hours, claiming 239 Houthi fighters neutralized and 117 military vehicles destroyed or damaged, according to a statement from spokesperson Majid al-Nuzaili carried by Xinhua and IANS. Government forces said they continued to consolidate gains in the southwestern province of Taiz. The Houthis, meanwhile, said Saudi forces carried out 101 air and missile strikes on Sanaa and eight provinces over the same 24 hours, claiming dozens dead or wounded, including women and children. Neither set of figures has been independently verified — access for independent journalists in Yemen remains severely restricted.
The civilian toll is contested in the same way. Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that at least 14 people were killed Wednesday in attacks on a public market and the nearby Al-Tayseer fuel station in Al-Hazm, the capital of northern Al-Jawf province, with 10 to 15 injured including women and children. Saudi authorities had not immediately responded to the allegation when initial reports were published. The same figure — 14 killed, 10 wounded — appeared in Wednesday evening reporting of a Saudi strike on Jawf/Al Hazm, but the two reports describe different target types, and the claims remain unverified.
On the Saudi side, the coalition said Thursday it intercepted a ballistic missile fired toward the kingdom's Eastern Province, spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X — a day after a Taif intercept. The Houthis said this week they had targeted the Ras Tanura refinery in the oil-rich Eastern Province. And fresh explosions were heard near Aden International Airport on Wednesday, shortly after Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree issued what he called a "final" evacuation warning, alleging — without evidence — that a Saudi military cargo aircraft was present transporting weapons. Hundreds of passengers, including patients, left the airport following the warnings; casualties and damage from the latest blasts were not immediately confirmed.
For ordinary Yemenis, this is the world's worst humanitarian crisis getting worse: humanitarian agencies warn escalations of this scale severely disrupt aid delivery, and the airport at Aden is the south's humanitarian lifeline. For everyone else, the fighting is one more reason oil stays near $114 and Red Sea shipping stays cautious.
In short: Yemen's ground war escalated sharply — 749 government strikes claimed against 101 Saudi strikes claimed — with 14 reported killed at an Al-Jawf market and fuel station, a Houthi missile intercepted over Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, and fresh blasts at Aden airport. Figures from both sides are unverified.
Sources:
Source: hiindia.com.

item.title: Israel's election settled nothing: Netanyahu ahead at 53 seats, no bloc near a majority
item.description:
Israel's election produced a clear winner of the night and no winner of the government. With nearly all ordinary ballots counted Thursday morning, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties held 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, according to Reuters and Israel's Central Elections Committee figures carried by multiple outlets, while Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc trailed on 48. Arab-led parties — the Joint List and Ra'am — surged to a combined 19 seats, nearly double their 10 in the outgoing Knesset and described by Israeli outlets as a historic high. Likud remained the largest single party at 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar at 21.
The arithmetic is the story: 61 seats are needed for a majority, and neither bloc reaches it. As the Council on Foreign Relations' Elliott Abrams wrote from Jerusalem on Thursday morning, Netanyahu's result is "both a defeat and a victory" — his outgoing coalition held 68 seats at its peak, so this is a real reduction, yet he is positioned to continue as prime minister because the president must ask the politician best situated to form a government to try, and that has to be Netanyahu. The question, Abrams notes, is where Netanyahu finds eight more seats: the opposition has promised not to serve in a new Netanyahu government, and Eisenkot has ruled out governing with Arab parties' support. If Netanyahu fails, President Isaac Herzog turns to Eisenkot — who faces the same wall from 48. The remaining path runs through broken campaign promises: a grand coalition, defectors, or a rotation deal — including the theory that Netanyahu, who just turned 77, might step aside in two years to seek the presidency when Herzog's term ends.
The count itself is not quite finished: roughly 430,000–480,000 double-envelope ballots, including soldiers' and reservists' votes, were still being counted overnight into Thursday, with final certified results expected around midday Thursday and the statutory publication deadline November 4. Turnout was 77.7%, the highest in over 20 years, with Arab turnout approaching 80%.
Markets have already voted on the uncertainty: the shekel weakened about 2% to 3.1185 to the dollar on Wednesday — its worst day in 16 months — and Tel Aviv's benchmark index fell around 3%, reversing gains made when high turnout had raised hopes of a change of government. Capital Economics' William Jackson said the next government "will probably be fragile," and failure by either leader to form one would likely mean another election, with Netanyahu remaining as caretaker in the meantime. For the region, CFR notes the foreign-policy stakes: on Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran there is broad Israeli consensus, but an Eisenkot government would be less likely to attack Iran soon simply because it would be new — while Netanyahu will likely soon ask President Trump about a renewed assault on Iran's nuclear sites.
In short: Netanyahu's bloc leads 53–48 with Arab parties holding a record 19, but nobody has the 61 seats needed to govern — so coalition bargaining, and possibly another election, comes next. Final certified results are expected Thursday.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Apple opened pre-orders for five new products, including its first touchscreen MacBooks and a new OLED iPad mini
item.description:
Apple opened pre-orders Wednesday for five new products, MacRumors reports: the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 ($1,999), the M6 iMac ($1,499), the new iPad mini with an 8.5-inch OLED display and A20 Pro chip ($699), and the first touchscreen MacBook Pros — 14-inch from $2,899 and 16-inch from $3,399, with M5 Pro/Max and a PROLED tandem OLED touch display.
The iPad mini, iMac and M6 MacBook Pro arrive November 6, as do the touchscreen models. The iPad mini is the genuinely new item here beyond the MacBook news already covered: larger OLED screen, nano-texture option, thinner and lighter design, IP67 water and dust resistance, a landscape front camera, and Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7.
Why it matters: it's Apple's cheapest route into the new OLED Mac lineup, and the touchscreen MacBooks are Apple's first ever — a product line that was rumored for years and finally real. Source:
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: Alphabet shares fell ~11% after its Q3 cash burn — but Google's TPU chip sales are now a real business
item.description:
Alphabet shares fell nearly 11% on Thursday after the company reported another quarter of cash burn and said AI infrastructure spending would rise sharply next year, Reuters reports.
The flip side, laid out by finance chief Anat Ashkenazi on the post-earnings call: Google's homegrown TPU chips, once reserved for internal use, are now sold to outside customers and made a "meaningful" contribution as Google Cloud revenue more than doubled in the September quarter (+103% to $30.7B). The catch is cash flow — unlike search or cloud, selling chip systems means spending on hardware well before customers pay, so inventory of unsold TPU systems is now showing up on the balance sheet.
TPU system sales are expected to rise further this quarter and ramp significantly in 2027. Why it matters: Google is now a genuine Nvidia challenger, not just a customer — and investors are pricing in how expensive that ambition is.
Source:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Nvidia signs study to put data centers on retired German nuclear sites
item.description:
Nvidia has signed a preliminary agreement with German nuclear operator PreussenElektra to study whether retired nuclear plant sites could be repurposed as large data centers, Softonic reports — using the land, grid links and cooling water already built around the plants, not restarting any reactors.
Germany shut its last operating reactors in April 2023 and has about 30 plants in closure or dismantling, eight of them PreussenElektra's. Still only a feasibility study, not a construction plan, and public support will hinge on renewables and environmental protections.
Source: Softonic (single source)
Source: en.softonic.com.

item.title: JetBrains' ThinkRail tops GitHub trending — an open-source IDE built around the pi coding agent
item.description:
ThinkRail, JetBrains' open-source IDE for "vibe coding" with the pi coding agent, was first on GitHub's daily trending list on October 28 with 4,585 stars, 1,075 added that day, according to Digital Soul Hub.
It's Apache-2.0, written in TypeScript, and runs pi in-process — pi owns models, skills and session state while ThinkRail provides the editor, files, terminals, git and agent workspaces. No accounts of its own; sign in with JetBrains AI or any provider pi supports.
Why it matters: it's JetBrains' answer to the agent-IDE wave, and it topped trending the day after GitHub Universe. Source:
Source: digisoulhub.com.

item.title: PHP2Shell federal patch deadline is today — and exploitation is spreading to firewall management interfaces
item.description:
Today, October 29, is the federal deadline CISA set for patching the critical PHP flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell, CVSS 9.2), added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26.
Palo Alto Networks now reports exploitation against internet-exposed firewall management interfaces, according to SecureResearch's October 29 daily brief, and Censys counted 32.5 million vulnerable PHP services as of October 27 against only about 11.2 million updated. Fixes are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 — updating Drupal or app code alone doesn't fix the runtime.
Why it matters: this is the week's biggest patching fire, and the deadline is today, not next week. Sources:
Source: secureresearch.com.

item.title: Russell Brand trial: wife Laura Brand gives evidence as cross-examination continues
item.description:
Laura Brand gave evidence Thursday in her husband's trial at Southwark Crown Court, The Times reports — describing him as "caring," "amazing" and "attentive," saying "I love him very much," and telling the court the pair got back together in 2015 and married in 2017.
Under cross-examination by prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC, she was pressed on a 2020 podcast in which she said she had not seen Brand "in years" before they got back together; she replied that "years could be a year and a half or two years" and that she had hung out with him many times. Brand himself spent Wednesday on the stand for more than four hours denying all seven charges (three rape, three sexual assault, one attempted indecent assault, six women, 1999–2009), admitting he "misused" fame for "reckless philandering" while insisting consent was non-negotiable.
Cross-examination continues. Sources:
Source: thetimes.com.

item.title: Israel's count is nearly done at 53–48–19 — and Thursday's leftover ballots decide what moves, if anything
item.description:
Israel's election count has moved from the evening's near-final picture to a nearly complete one, and the headline has not changed: Benjamin Netanyahu leads, nobody has a majority, and the next step belongs to the ballots not yet counted. A live tracker updated October 29 put the count at 98.17% of ballots, with the Netanyahu bloc at 53 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's Change bloc at 48, and the Arab parties at 19 — the same 53–48–19 split as the evening brief, now on a near-complete count. Double-envelope ballots — soldiers' votes and others — are counted Thursday, with definitive results expected Thursday and official results by November 4, so parties near the 3.25% threshold can still shift the margins.
Reuters' Wednesday account frames the result as a paradox that both camps are now spinning in opposite directions. Netanyahu, described by a former adviser as staging a political "resurrection," has restored his primacy even while losing his majority — and in his post-election speech he called for a "strong, right-wing national government" and a renewed joint move against Iran with the United States, calling it a "singular historical opportunity." President Donald Trump, who had urged Israelis to keep Netanyahu in power to "finish the job" in Iran, said the prime minister had done "very well" and credited his own endorsement. Eisenkot, for his part, has acknowledged Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister but says he has lost public support, has urged him to retire, and has warned security chiefs to resist political pressure. Analysts quoted by Reuters see two broad paths out: a broader unity government led by Netanyahu — potentially bringing in Eisenkot or Naftali Bennett — or another election in 2027, which several analysts said could strengthen Netanyahu further rather than change the outcome.
The other side of the story is the Arab parties, whose unprecedentedly high turnout handed them their decisive position. Reuters notes Arab Israelis — 21% of the population — have "never been in a position where they held this much power," in the words of former US negotiator Dennis Ross, and a tracker of the count reports Arab-led lists signalling openness to helping form an alternative government. The catch, Reuters stresses, is that Eisenkot's route to power likely requires direct or indirect Arab support, a prospect that could prove difficult for potential right-wing partners such as Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman — and both main camps have so far ruled out relying on them. Meanwhile the Gulf is already pricing the uncertainty: Reuters' Gulf analysis notes Brent crude at $115 a barrel on Wednesday, with Riyadh's airport disruption (86% of flights cancelled across October 8–25, per Cirium) still hanging over the region.

Israel's election count has moved from the evening's near-final picture to a nearly complete one, and the headline has not changed: Benjamin Netanyahu leads, nobody has a majority, and the next step belongs to the ballots not yet counted. A live tracker updated October 29 put the count at 98.17% of ballots, with the Netanyahu bloc at 53 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's Change bloc at 48, and the Arab parties at 19 — the same 53–48–19 split as the evening brief, now on a near-complete count. Double-envelope ballots — soldiers' votes and others — are counted Thursday, with definitive results expected Thursday and official results by November 4, so parties near the 3.25% threshold can still shift the margins.

Reuters' Wednesday account frames the result as a paradox that both camps are now spinning in opposite directions. Netanyahu, described by a former adviser as staging a political "resurrection," has restored his primacy even while losing his majority — and in his post-election speech he called for a "strong, right-wing national government" and a renewed joint move against Iran with the United States, calling it a "singular historical opportunity." President Donald Trump, who had urged Israelis to keep Netanyahu in power to "finish the job" in Iran, said the prime minister had done "very well" and credited his own endorsement. Eisenkot, for his part, has acknowledged Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister but says he has lost public support, has urged him to retire, and has warned security chiefs to resist political pressure. Analysts quoted by Reuters see two broad paths out: a broader unity government led by Netanyahu — potentially bringing in Eisenkot or Naftali Bennett — or another election in 2027, which several analysts said could strengthen Netanyahu further rather than change the outcome.

The other side of the story is the Arab parties, whose unprecedentedly high turnout handed them their decisive position. Reuters notes Arab Israelis — 21% of the population — have "never been in a position where they held this much power," in the words of former US negotiator Dennis Ross, and a tracker of the count reports Arab-led lists signalling openness to helping form an alternative government. The catch, Reuters stresses, is that Eisenkot's route to power likely requires direct or indirect Arab support, a prospect that could prove difficult for potential right-wing partners such as Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman — and both main camps have so far ruled out relying on them. Meanwhile the Gulf is already pricing the uncertainty: Reuters' Gulf analysis notes Brent crude at $115 a barrel on Wednesday, with Riyadh's airport disruption (86% of flights cancelled across October 8–25, per Cirium) still hanging over the region.

For ordinary Israelis, the practical consequence is a stretch of caretaker government while President Isaac Herzog consults the party groups — with the Iran confrontation, the Gaza aftermath and Netanyahu's own corruption trial all sitting with a government that has lost its old majority. For everyone else in the region, the question is whether Netanyahu's lead hardens into a government that can move on Iran after the US midterms on November 3, as the New York Post's observers now expect.

In short: the count is now 98.17% complete at 53–48–19, the Arab parties hold the balance and are signalling openness to a change government, and Thursday's double-envelope ballots plus Herzog's consultations are the next real events — not another projection.

item.title: Hormuz: US Central Command calls Iran's mine claims "FALSE."
item.content:encoded:
In an October 28 post, CENTCOM dismissed Iranian media reports that commercial vessels are striking sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, saying all internationally recognized primary transit routes have been cleared of mines by US forces and remain so, and that thousands of vessels continue to pass safely.

That directly contradicts Iran's army claim Tuesday that a tanker running dark hit mines and caught fire east of the strait — the two sides' accounts of the waterway are now in open dispute, days before Iran's threatened November 1 "legal action" against Sinokor tankers. item.title: Ukraine: independent assessment confirms the steel and chemical plant fires
item.description:

item.title: Alphabet's cloud doubled — and the market still sold it off 9%
item.description:
Alphabet reported third-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, and the quarter split cleanly in two: an operating business that beat expectations in the cloud, and a spending bill that spooked investors. According to the earnings release Alphabet filed with the SEC, revenue for the quarter ended September 30 rose 25% to $127.6 billion, the 13th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, and operating income rose 30% to $40.6 billion. Google Cloud was the star: revenue jumped 103% to $30.7 billion, with operating income more than tripling to $11.1 billion, led by enterprise AI infrastructure and TPU system sales, according to Securities.io's read of the release. Search grew 12% to $63.4 billion, YouTube ads 9% to $11.2 billion, and CEO Sundar Pichai said the company is "now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate," with the Gemini app at one billion users.
The other side of the ledger is why the stock fell about 9% in after-hours trading, to around $293–294 from a $324.89 close. Capital expenditures hit $51.4 billion in a single quarter — more than double a year earlier — pushing free cash flow to negative $9.07 billion, far worse than the roughly flat figure analysts expected, according to CNBC market data carried by SourceFirstNews. Net income available to common shareholders fell 25% to $26.2 billion, or $2.12 per share, missing estimates, but much of that was an $8.7 billion paper loss on equity securities, not operations. Alphabet also sold $12.4 billion of stock, raised $28.7 billion in notes, and repurchased no shares in the quarter — a financing posture that reads as a company funding its AI build-out with other people's money while it lasts.
For ordinary users, the practical upshot is less about the share price than about where the money is going: Google's AI infrastructure spending is now running at a pace that outstrips the cash the business generates, for a second straight quarter. The bull case is that Cloud's doubling proves the spending is already paying off in enterprise AI revenue. The bear case is that a $51 billion quarterly capex run rate, if sustained, is a bet that AI demand keeps doubling too — and the market, at least overnight, priced the risk rather than the growth.
In short: Cloud doubled and operating income rose 30%, but a $51.4 billion capex quarter drove free cash flow to negative $9.1 billion and the stock down ~9% after hours. Watch Thursday's analyst calls and whether the sell-off holds into the regular session.
Sources: Securities.io, October 28; SourceFirstNews/CNBC, October 28; TickerRoast, October 28

item.title: Google opens Gemini and Search to third-party apps
item.description:
Google opened a US public preview of its Connected Apps Platform on October 28, letting any developer submit an app to work inside Gemini and Google Search via a cloud MCP server or Android AppFunctions, with review and usage tracking in a new Google Connected Console.
Adobe, Experian, Localiza and Peloton are due in Search in the coming weeks; Calm launches on both. Previously only Google-picked partners (Canva, YouTube Music) appeared as connected apps.
Why it matters: Google is turning its AI surfaces into a distribution channel like an app store — who gets inside the chatbot becomes the new homepage fight. Sources: TechCrunch, October 28;
Source: techcrunch.com.

item.title: Node2Shell: Brotli decoder flaw added to CISA's exploited list, deadline November 10
item.description:
CISA added CVE-2026-111497 (Google Brotli decoder, CVSS 9.2) to KEV on Tuesday after honeypot hits and live exploit traffic observed by ELLIO and Previdian, with Imperva demonstrating RCE in a vulnerable Node.js image.
An unauthenticated attacker can corrupt decoder memory via a crafted Brotli stream, potentially reaching remote code execution. Node.js, PHP, Bun, Envoy, Istio, .NET and Python have all issued patches or advisories — update binaries, rebuild container images and restart services; there is no single runtime workaround.
Sources: Particle News, October 28;
Source: particle.news.

item.title: Netanyahu's lead holds as the count nears completion — but still no majority
item.description:
Israel's election count has moved from the morning's partial picture to a near-final one, and the headline has not changed: Benjamin Netanyahu is leading, and nobody has a majority. With about 85% of ballots counted, projections gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, short of the 61 needed to govern, according to one Wednesday report; a live tracker with 97.63% counted put it at 53 for Netanyahu's bloc, 48 for the Change bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, and 19 for the Arab parties. Likud itself is the largest single party, with about 26 seats on roughly 21% of the vote, ahead of Eisenkot's Yashar on about 21. The remaining double-envelope ballots — soldiers' votes and others — are due to be counted from Wednesday night into Thursday, with definitive results expected Thursday and official results by November 4, so the seat numbers can still shift at the margins, particularly for parties near the 3.25% threshold.
The two camps are drawing opposite conclusions from the same count. Netanyahu, who called overnight for a "strong, right-wing national government," has also raised the prospect of a renewed joint move against Iran with the United States, calling it a "singular historical opportunity" — and the New York Post reports that observers now see a third act for the Iran war as almost certain if he stays, with one INSS Iran expert quoted as saying Tehran fears Netanyahu precisely because he talks about attacking Iran again. Eisenkot, for his part, has acknowledged Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister but says he has lost public support, has urged him to retire from politics, and has warned him not to use security for political purposes. President Isaac Herzog, who will consult the party groups before choosing who gets the first attempt at forming a government, has urged leaders to consider different options and avoid another election.
For ordinary Israelis, the practical consequence is a stretch of caretaker government while coalition talks drag on — with the Iran confrontation, the Gaza aftermath and Netanyahu's own corruption trial all sitting with a government that has lost its old majority. The Arab parties, at 18–19 seats and nearly double their 2022 result, hold the balance of power in arithmetic terms even though both main camps have so far ruled out relying on them; Eisenkot has resisted governing with them, and Netanyahu has rejected a government backed by them. If neither bloc can assemble 61 seats, another election in 2027 becomes likely.
In short: the count is nearly done and Netanyahu leads 53–48–19, but no bloc reaches 61, the Arab parties hold the balance, and the decisive questions — who gets the mandate from Herzog, and whether Netanyahu's lead hardens into a government that can move on Iran — come after Thursday's near-final result.
Sources: Live tracker, October 28; Harava, October 28; New York Post, October 28; Reuters Breakingviews, October 28
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*

item.title: Aden airport hit twice in one day as the Yemen war's civilian toll climbs
item.description:
The Houthi war against Saudi Arabia and Yemen's government escalated again on Wednesday, with Aden International Airport — the main gateway for the government-held south — hit twice in a single day. Houthi missiles targeted the airport twice on October 28, the first while a Saudi military plane was on the ground; police said the plane left unharmed, according to one report. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree had earlier ordered an immediate evacuation of the airport, alleging a Saudi cargo plane was moving weapons through it. The airport has now been attacked four times this month, including two ballistic missiles on October 24, and Médecins Sans Frontières said one of its aircraft was about to take off from Aden a few days ago when humanitarian workers were told to seek shelter as a missile struck nearby — the charity stressed that safe access to the airport is crucial because it is the main entry point for humanitarian workers, supplies and medical equipment to southern Yemen.
The other side of Wednesday's ledger came from Houthi-run media, which reported Saudi airstrikes on Al Hazm in the northern Jawf region killing 14 people and wounding 10, with women and children among the reported casualties — a toll that is preliminary and comes from Houthi sources, not independently verified. Reuters' own Wednesday account, carried by regional outlets, confirms the Aden strikes and the evacuation warning, and notes the renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that had largely halted major attacks in the conflict. Aid agencies warn the latest violence is rapidly worsening conditions in a country already suffering from one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with nearly 260,000 people reported displaced across Yemen since August.
For ordinary people, the airport attacks hit twice over: they endanger the humanitarian lifeline into the south, and they sit alongside the Saudi-side strikes that have now killed a reported 20+ people in the past week of airport attacks, plus the debris damage in Riyadh from interceptions. The Houthis present the Aden strikes as attacks on a military target; the government and aid agencies present them as a threat to civil aviation and to the aid pipeline. Neither framing changes the immediate fact: flights, aid and medical evacuations through Aden are now operating under repeated missile warnings.
In short: Aden airport was hit twice on Wednesday with an evacuation order, Houthi media report 14 killed in a Saudi strike on Jawf, and the airport — the south's humanitarian lifeline — is now a recurring target. Watch whether flights and aid movements through Aden continue or halt, and whether the coalition responds in kind.
Sources: Reuters via 947 The Beast, October 28; Europesays/Türkiye, October 28; Silent Dossier, October 28
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*

item.title: Kharkiv hit twice in 24 hours as Ukraine strikes Russian steel and chemical plants
item.description:
The war's long-range exchange continued on both sides on Wednesday. In Kharkiv, a Russian drone strike around 1 p.m. local time hit the Osnovianskyi district, killing a 60-year-old man and injuring three others, according to regional head Oleh Syniehubov as reported by Ukrinform — the second strike on the same neighbourhood in 24 hours, after a jet-powered drone late Tuesday evening set fires across some 2,500 square metres of residential and industrial terrain, injuring five people including a four-year-old child. City officials condemned the consecutive attacks on a single district, noting first responders had spent hours clearing the scene between the two strikes under dangerous, exposed conditions.
Ukraine, meanwhile, launched a major overnight drone attack into Russia on the night of October 27–28, targeting the country's largest steel plant and a chemical facility, according to the National Security Journal and other reports. Fires were reported at industrial sites in Lipetsk and Tula regions, with Ukrainian monitoring channels reporting a fire near the Novolipetsk Steel Plant and flames at the Novomoskovsk Azot chemical plant, one of Russia's largest nitrogen fertilizer makers. Moscow claimed to have intercepted more than 500 Ukrainian drones; Lipetsk's governor said 45 drones were shot down over his region and downplayed reports of a major industrial fire, attributing a fire to debris igniting in a wooded area. Ukraine has not formally claimed responsibility, and the full extent of the damage is still unclear — the two sides' accounts diverge sharply, as they usually do on strike damage.
The human impact runs in both directions. In Kharkiv, the repeated strikes on one district mean residents and responders are being hit while still clearing the previous attack. In Russia, the targeting of steel and fertilizer production is aimed at industrial capacity, but debris from interceptions damaged an apartment building in Lipetsk, according to the governor's own account. On the front itself, Ukraine's General Staff reported 191 combat engagements over the past day, with Russian losses claimed at 1,510 personnel — figures from one side, unverified independently. The Oleshky humanitarian operation remains the scheduled test for Thursday and Friday: demining Thursday, aid from October 29, evacuations planned Friday.
In short: Kharkiv's Osnovianskyi district was hit twice in a day, Ukraine hit back at Russian steel and chemical plants overnight with damage still disputed, and the front-line fighting has not eased. Watch Thursday for whether the Oleshky demining actually happens — that, more than the strike claims, is the next verifiable event.
Sources: Europesays/Ukrinform, October 28; National Security Journal, October 28; SSBCrack, October 28
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Hormuz: Iran threatens the tankers carrying 40% of the strait's oil
item.description:
Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority said it will take "legal action" against all vessels of Sinokor — the world's largest supertanker owner, whose ships carried nearly 40% of the crude flowing out of Hormuz last month — starting November 1, citing the highest number of crossing violations over three months and saying enforcement actions have already been taken against at least seven of its vessels.
Sinokor did not immediately respond. Separately, US Naval Forces Central Command advised on October 28 that vessels with no need to transit the Hormuz/Gulf of Oman area should stay well clear, and warned of extra transit time for blockade enforcement — the first such advisory since mid-July.
Sources: Rigzone/Bloomberg, October 28;
Source: rigzone.com.

item.title: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook is real — and $400 dearer than the model it sits above
item.description:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook, ending years in which the company insisted it would not combine the iPad and Mac experiences. At its "Pro and tell" event in Los Angeles, Apple debuted the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, with a tandem OLED touchscreen, a Dynamic Island replacing the notch, and the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the MacBook Pros announced in March, according to MacRumors and USA Today. The display offers up to 2,000 nits of HDR and SDR brightness, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and ProMotion refresh from 10Hz to 120Hz, with an optional nano-texture finish. A touch sensor built directly into the display panel means no added latency, Apple says, and macOS automatically translates touch into clicks, so many existing apps work with touch right away — Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, Adobe Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve and Blender are named as already compatible.
The pricing is where the two sides of the story meet. The 14-inch starts at $2,899 and the 16-inch at $3,399, with M5 Max configurations from $4,499 and $4,799 respectively — $400 above the mini-LED models they sit alongside, which Apple is keeping in the lineup for now, as is the separate $1,999 M6 14-inch MacBook Pro announced Tuesday. The new machines are lighter (three pounds for the 14-inch, four for the 16-inch), up to 1mm slimmer, with a redesigned hinge for touch stability, up to 128GB of unified memory, up to 16TB of storage, a six-speaker system with 50% deeper bass, three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, SDXC, MagSafe, Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, and up to 24 hours of battery life. Pre-orders opened Wednesday, with launch on Friday, November 6.
For ordinary buyers, the practical question is whether touch is worth the premium: Apple positions it as an additional input alongside keyboard and trackpad, not a replacement, and the machines run the same M5 Pro/Max silicon as the March models — so the $400 buys the display, the touch layer, the thinner chassis and the Dynamic Island, not faster chips. For professionals who already live in the named touch-compatible apps, the pitch is a real workflow change; for everyone else, the kept-alive mini-LED models and the $1,999 M6 machine are the cheaper way into a new MacBook Pro.
In short: Apple's first touchscreen Mac is here, it is a genuine reversal of a long-held position, and it costs $400 more than the equivalent non-touch model for the same chips. Pre-orders are open now, machines land November 6 — the first hands-on reviews will say whether the touch layer earns its premium.
Sources: MacRumors, October 28;
Source: images.macrumors.com.

item.title: OpenAI reportedly plans to buy Google's AI chips
item.description:
Reuters, citing The Information, reports OpenAI plans to purchase Google TPUs to reduce reliance on Nvidia — a plan, not a finished deal: no price, volume, chip generation or timing disclosed, and OpenAI declined to comment to Reuters.
OpenAI already rents Google chips through Google Cloud and is hiring engineers to optimize its frontier models for TPUs. Treat as reported, not confirmed.

item.title: DeepTutor: an open-source AI tutor you run yourself
item.description:
DeepTutor is an agent-native learning workspace — chat, quizzes, research, course study, audio overviews and inspectable memory in one runtime, with YouTube/Bilibili transcript-grounded tutoring and subagents via Claude Code/Codex.
Apache-2.0, Python, 44,833 GitHub stars as of October 28, latest release v1.6.15 from October 19. Why it matters: it is a self-hosted alternative to closed AI tutors, and the shared session context across study modes is the part most tutors do not offer.
Source:
Source: digisoulhub.com.

item.title: Fragnesia: Linux kernel flaw added to CISA's exploited list, deadline Saturday
item.description:
CISA added CVE-2026-46300 (Linux kernel, dubbed Fragnesia) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 28, with a federal deadline of October 31.
Per SecurityWeek/The Hacker News via the daily threat brief, attackers are chaining it with the PHP2Shell flaws to plant PHP webshells and escalate to root; security firm Dream says a suspected China-linked group used the chain against 25 internet-facing firewalls on October 23–24, then used two of them to reach into a US government-affiliated network and target Active Directory. If you run Linux servers with PHP, patch PHP and the kernel and reboot so the new kernel actually runs.
Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: Brand under cross-examination: "reckless philandering" admitted, key details disputed
item.description:
Russell Brand's defence case moved into its testing phase on Wednesday at Southwark Crown Court, as prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC cross-examined him after his morning evidence in chief. Brand, 51, denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault involving six women between 1999 and 2009. Under cross-examination he admitted he had "misused" his fame for "reckless philandering," telling the court he had been "persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless, philandering and idiocy" — while insisting consent was "non-negotiable" and that he never forced himself on a woman. He also admitted he was "obsessed" with sex in his younger years but denied being unable to function without it, and denied pretending to be gay to make women trust him.
The prosecution's line of attack, as reported by The Times and The Guardian, is that Brand's account has shifted. Karmy-Jones pressed him on alleged inconsistencies between his defence statement and his testimony about the alleged 2009 anal rape of Woman 5, including details such as sex toys and "sexual talk" that he said he recollected after seeing her witness statement. Brand conceded the point in striking terms: "Since these events occurred, there's been escalating recollection. It's been a deeply traumatic episode of my life I have focused on at the expense of my marriage, my children and health. I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that." He also rejected a former friend's claim that he had a goal of sleeping with 5,000 women — "No, not a goal" — and said he did not recall the conversation in question. On the origins of the case, he said he blamed the Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and Times/Sunday Times reporting for the allegations, answering "Yes" when asked if he blamed the documentary, and "In some ways" when pressed on blaming the media generally.
The two framings now in front of the jury are clear. The prosecution presents a man whose recollections grew after reading the evidence, whose admitted pursuit of women was relentless, and whose defence rests on consent in encounters the complainants describe very differently. The defence presents a man whose younger behaviour was reckless but consensual, whose life has been consumed by the case — he told the court in the morning that not a single person would give evidence on his behalf — and who argues the publicity itself shaped the prosecution. Neither framing settles the seven counts; the jury must decide each one separately, and Brand spent about four hours on the stand on Wednesday, with cross-examination continuing.
In short: Brand admitted misusing fame for reckless philandering but denied every charge, conceded his recollections contain inconsistencies, and blamed the 2023 documentary for the case — and the cross-examination, not his morning statement, is where the defence case is now being tested.
Sources: The Times, October 28; The Guardian live account via ByteSeu, October 28; Wansom, October 28
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: thetimes.com.
