item.title: Netanyahu's bloc gains as the count moves on — but still no majority
item.description:
Israel woke up on Wednesday to a count that has moved in Benjamin Netanyahu's favour since the exit polls, without giving anyone a government. With about 71–77% of votes tallied in the morning, Israeli media projected Netanyahu's right-wing bloc at 54 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc at 47, and Arab-led parties at 19, according to Reuters — still seven seats short of the 61 needed in the 120-seat Knesset. Later partial counts put the same split at 54–47–19 with 76.8% of ballot boxes counted, and one tracker had it at 54–49–17 with 84.66% counted. The count is not final: more than half a million double-envelope ballots, including soldiers' votes, are due to be counted from Wednesday night into Thursday evening, with definitive results expected Thursday and official results due by November 4.
The two camps are reading the same numbers in opposite ways. Netanyahu told supporters overnight that Israel must form a "strong, right-wing national government," and, according to France 24, ruled out a government backed by Arab parties. He also raised the prospect of a renewed joint move against Iran with the United States, calling it a "singular historical opportunity." Eisenkot said "the people have spoken against the continuation of Netanyahu's rule," warned against another election, and has warned Netanyahu not to use security for political purposes. Democrats leader Yair Golan went further, writing that "Netanyahu lost" — counting the opposition and Arab-led lists together. The Arab parties are the night's clear gainers: Le Monde reports their two lists could win at least 18 seats, nearly double their 2022 result, driven by record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, and their leader Mansour Abbas said the turnout reflected "despair and frustration that has turned into hope."
The market reaction was swift and negative. Reuters reports the shekel weakened about 2% to 3.1185 to the dollar, on track for its worst day in 16 months, reversing Tuesday's gains that had been driven by hopes of a change of government; Tel Aviv's benchmark index fell around 3%, and yields on the 10-year government bond rose. Capital Economics' William Jackson said the initial results offered more paths for Netanyahu to remain in power, "though any government that emerged was unlikely to be robust," and added: "The next government will probably be fragile." That matters beyond the markets: until a government is formed, Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister, and if neither bloc can assemble 61 seats, another election in 2027 becomes likely.
For ordinary Israelis, the practical upshot is a longer stretch of caretaker government while coalition talks drag on — with the Iran confrontation, the Gaza aftermath and Netanyahu's own corruption trial all sitting with a government that has lost its old majority. The Arab parties, courted by neither bloc so far, now hold the balance of power in arithmetic terms, even if both main camps have ruled out relying on them.
In short: the count moved toward Netanyahu but stopped short of a majority, the Arab parties nearly doubled their representation, markets sold off on the prospect of a fragile government, and the decisive ballots — the double-envelope votes — are still to be counted. Watch Thursday's near-final result and who gets the first attempt at forming a government.
Sources: Reuters, October 28; Le Monde, October 28; Bullquill live count, October 28
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Washington tells Gulf allies to prepare for a possible post-midterms strike on Iran — but no decision yet
item.description:
The United States has told several Gulf Arab states to prepare for a possible "short, intense" military campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people briefed on the conversations. The reporting, carried by multiple outlets on Wednesday morning, says President Trump has not made a final decision but is leaning toward a major post-election strike aimed at Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, intended to force Tehran back to the negotiating table. The White House declined to comment on "sensitive military plans that may or may not happen," saying only that Trump "is keeping all options available and ensuring that Iran will never possess a nuclear weapon."
The reported preparations are concrete on the US side. According to the Journal's account, US forces are replenishing ammunition and readying fighter jets and bombers, a Patriot battery has been moved from Texas to the region, troops have been repositioned away from bases vulnerable to retaliation, and an additional carrier strike group and Marine expeditionary unit are expected to join the roughly 20 warships already in the Middle East. Separately, The Hill reports that US Central Command has strike options ready to present to War Secretary Pete Hegseth if the White House authorises them, and that Trump "will leave all of his options open until he has to make the final decision." Analysts quoted in that reporting warn of the other side of the ledger: Iran still holds large drone and missile stocks and can hit Gulf shipping, oil facilities and US bases, so any new round carries a high risk of retaliation.
Tehran's position, as reported in recent days, is that it wants a deal on its own terms — including over control of the Strait of Hormuz — and has threatened regional targets if war resumes. Gulf governments, meanwhile, face the immediate dilemma: prepare for a campaign they did not ask for, while diplomatic efforts involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey continue in parallel. The Journal's reporting notes that Trump has previously said he would not strike Iran before the midterms, and that he has weighed holding off if ceasefire negotiations were possible — but that slow progress in mediated talks has pushed him toward the strike option. One analyst, Gregory Brew of Eurasia Group, put it bluntly: "it looks pretty likely that the U.S. goes back to military strikes on Iran once the midterm elections are passed."
For ordinary people, the most immediate effect is already visible at the pump and in markets: Brent crude rose past $115 a barrel on Wednesday on the combination of this reporting and the Houthi attacks below, and Gulf states have already begun drawing down non-essential embassy staff in some posts. A short, intense campaign is not a contained one if Iran answers against shipping or oil infrastructure — the pattern of the last eight months suggests escalation spreads fast, and oil is the transmission mechanism to everyone else's fuel and food prices.
In short: the warning to Gulf allies is real and widely reported, the military preparations are under way, but the strike itself is not authorised — the decision point is after November 3, and the next signals to watch are any Trump statement, any Iranian response, and whether the mediated talks produce anything before then.
Sources: Wall Street Journal reporting via Aju Press, October 28; The Hill via Arutz Sheva, October 28; Particle News, October 28
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: ajupress.com.

item.title: Missiles at Taif and Aden, a refinery claim Riyadh won't confirm — and oil past $115
item.description:
The Houthi war against Saudi Arabia produced another overnight round on Wednesday, and oil markets reacted before the smoke cleared. The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Taif, in the mountains east of Mecca, early Wednesday, with no casualties or damage reported from that interception, while Civil Defense briefly raised and then lifted alerts in Jeddah and Yanbu on the Red Sea coast. Separately, a Houthi missile fell within the perimeter of Aden International Airport on Wednesday, according to police cited by Eagle Intel Reports, after which Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree ordered an evacuation of the facility, alleging a Saudi military cargo plane was moving weapons through it. Yemeni government media say two Houthi ballistic missiles targeted Aden airport on October 24 as well — the fourth such attack that month.
The market-moving claim came on Tuesday: the Houthis said they struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery — the kingdom's largest, at 550,000 barrels a day, and a major crude-export hub — with a ballistic missile. The Wall Street Journal and Morningstar both report that Aramco did not immediately respond and Saudi authorities have not confirmed a direct hit or any damage, though one report noted a fire near Aramco facilities at Ras Tanura had been contained. The coalition did confirm intercepting three ballistic missiles aimed at the Eastern Province and four drones aimed at the south on Tuesday, with Civil Defense reporting damage from falling debris in Riyadh. The gap between claim and confirmation matters: traders are pricing the risk, not a verified outage. December Brent rose to about $115–116 a barrel on Wednesday, up roughly 1–2%, and WTI to about $101–102, after falling nearly $2 on Tuesday on hopes that talks involving Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iran might ease tensions.
The two sides' accounts diverge in a familiar pattern. The Houthis present the strikes as pressure on Saudi oil and military infrastructure, and have vowed continued attacks on airports and oil facilities. The coalition presents its interceptions as successful defence and says it has struck Houthi launchers, storage tunnels and a missile depot in Yemen — claims that are unverified. Houthi-run media, meanwhile, reported Saudi airstrikes on the coastal city of Al-Mokha on Wednesday. Civilians sit in the middle of both stories: airport closures and evacuation warnings disrupt travel and aid, debris from interceptions damages buildings in Riyadh, and every unconfirmed refinery claim moves the oil price that sets fuel costs far beyond the Gulf.
In short: Taif was intercepted, Aden airport was hit and ordered evacuated, the Ras Tanura refinery strike is claimed but unconfirmed, and oil is up sharply on the risk rather than on verified damage. Watch for any Saudi or Aramco statement on Ras Tanura — that, more than the next claim, is what will move prices next.
Sources: Wall Street Journal via Morningstar, October 28; Eagle Intel Reports, October 28; Coalition account via blog report, October 28
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: morningstar.com.

item.title: Ukraine: a quieter night, a staged plan for Oleshky, and Kyiv building around its broken bridges
item.description:
After the heavy barrage of the night into Tuesday, the night into Wednesday was quieter — but the war's logistics campaign has not stopped, and Kyiv is now planning around it. Ukraine's Air Force morning report, as tallied by one open-source roundup, counted 88 drones launched overnight into Wednesday (71 downed) and one Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missile, with hits at 8 locations — down sharply from Tuesday night's 280 drones and up to 16 ballistic missiles. That is still a night of strikes, not a pause: the week to Wednesday morning totals 787 drones launched and at least 26 civilians killed and 261 injured in strikes reported by Ukrainian officials, according to the same roundup. Russia and Ukraine both deny deliberately targeting civilians; the figures are Ukrainian official counts and have not been independently verified.
The other track is the Oleshky operation, which now has a timetable. The local ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky took effect at 3 a.m. Tuesday, was widened beyond the town to parts of the Kherson region for convoy movement, and is due to last until November 1, according to a senior Ukrainian official cited by Roic News. The plan is staged: roads are to be cleared of mines on Thursday, with the humanitarian mission itself starting October 29 and civilian evacuations planned for Friday, according to earlier reporting confirmed in the new accounts. Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets says Kyiv is honouring its commitments, and Russia's defence ministry says it has stopped shelling toward Kherson to facilitate the operation. Fox News' inside account adds that the mission will be led by civilians from both countries — keeping the two militaries apart — and that four Newsmax journalists will accompany it to document residents' choices. Residents themselves, quoted in the coverage, fear they may not be allowed to return to Ukrainian-held territory, or may have their phones examined for signs of Ukrainian support; the Russian-installed Kherson head claims most want to leave for Russia, an account that could not be independently verified.
Kyiv, meanwhile, is adapting to the bridge campaign rather than waiting for it to end. Reuters reports the city plans to allocate 1 billion hryvnias (about $22 million) to build water crossings over the Dnipro — pontoons, fords or similar low structures — after Tuesday's ballistic strike closed the Southern Bridge to road and metro traffic. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's defence council discussed the crossings and access roads, though he gave no further details. Kyiv has six main bridges, and October has seen repeated strikes on them, disrupting travel for hundreds of thousands of people who live and work on opposite banks. The Finnish and Norwegian leaders' Tuesday phone call to Putin, already reported, drew a familiar response: Støre said afterwards that big differences remained, and the Kremlin's position — that any settlement must account for Russia's "legitimate interests" — is unchanged.
In short: a quieter night is not a ceasefire, Oleshky's real test comes Thursday and Friday when demining and evacuations are due to happen, and Kyiv is spending on river crossings because it expects the bridge strikes to continue. Watch whether aid actually moves into Oleshky on Thursday, and whether the Abu Dhabi technical talks in early November produce anything beyond a meeting.
Sources: Air Force tally via Substack roundup, October 28; Reuters on Kyiv water crossings, October 27; Roic News on Oleshky timetable, October 27; Fox News inside account, October 28
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: enlightentheday.substack.com.

item.title: Iran/Hormuz:
item.description:
Iran's army said on Tuesday that an unidentified oil tanker struck naval mines and caught fire east of the Strait of Hormuz while crossing, it said, on an unauthorised route with its tracking switched off.
No vessel name, flag, crew count or casualty figure was given, and the claim has not been independently verified — it also directly challenges US Central Command's earlier assertion that the strait's main lanes had been cleared of mines. Treat as an Iranian military claim, not a confirmed sinking.
Sources: ABNA, October 28;

item.title: Oracle will rent out Google's AI chips — from 2027
item.description:
At Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on October 27, Oracle and Google said Google's TPUs will be offered on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, billed as the first hyperscaler outside Google to offer them — TPU 8t for training and 8i for inference, arriving in calendar 2027 and ramping over several years.
Oracle also expanded its Nvidia Vera Rubin systems to "multi-gigawatt scale" (no deal value disclosed) and will add Cerebras and SambaNova inference hardware. The pitch is chip neutrality: buyers won't have to pick a cloud based on which silicon they want — but nothing here ships before 2027.
Sources: AI Stock Wire, October 28;
Source: aistockwire.com.

item.title: DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer, its production inference engine — with pieces held back
item.description:
DeepInfer, released October 20 under Apache 2.0, is the inference framework behind DeepSeek's production services, serving its DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash model.
It ships production kernels, speculative decoding (DSpark) and deterministic sampling — but, as the project's own README states, it covers offline inference only, leaving out the KV-cache layer, prefill/decode disaggregation and load balancing a full online service needs. It currently supports Nvidia SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs only, so it's a study and infrastructure-team release, not a drop-in vLLM replacement.
Sources: EduFabTech, October 27;
Source: edufabtech.com.

item.content:encoded:

If you run anything on Brotli 1.0.3–1.2.0, this is no longer a theoretical patch. Sources: The Hacker News, October 28;

item.title: Brand takes the stand: "No" — and says the allegations consumed his life
item.description:
Russell Brand took the witness box on Wednesday at Southwark Crown Court in London, the first day of his defence, and answered his own lawyer's central question loudly and clearly: asked whether he had committed any of the alleged crimes, he said "no." Brand, 51, faces three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault involving six women between 1999 and 2009, and denies all seven charges. Prosecutors, who completed their case earlier on Wednesday, have described him as a sexual predator; the defence case now has to answer that framing, not just deny it.
Brand's testimony so far has been about impact rather than the individual allegations. He told the jury the 2023 documentary and newspaper investigation that preceded the charges had a "devastating" effect: friends and colleagues turned against him, and, he said, not a single person would give evidence on his behalf — asked by his lawyer Ian Winter whether they would "touch you with a bargepole," he replied: "No." He said he was barred from the hospital where his son was receiving open-heart surgery after the documentary aired, and that his "entire life has been consumed by these events." On the substance, he told the court that consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed more important than sex itself," and that the first complainant had willingly had sex with him. The jury has previously been told all six complainants came forward to detectives after the 2023 documentary and related reporting — a point the defence is likely to press, and prosecutors will counter by arguing that coming forward after publicity does not undermine the accounts themselves.
The human stakes here cut both ways, and the trial's structure reflects that. For the complainants, the case is about allegations spanning a decade, now tested in cross-examination after nearly two weeks of prosecution evidence. For Brand, the defence opening is an argument that public ruin preceded — and shaped — the criminal case, and that the absence of defence witnesses is itself evidence of that pressure. Neither framing settles the charges; the jury's job is the specific counts, not the broader public argument. The judge has already amended one charge, downgrading indecent assault to attempted indecent assault for lack of evidence on the original form.
In short: Brand is now testifying, he denies everything, and his defence so far rests on the devastating personal cost of the allegations and the claim that no one will stand up for him in court. The trial continues, with cross-examination to come — that, more than the opening statement, is where the defence case will be tested.
Sources: Reuters via Duke FM, October 28; Guardian account via Suara Garut, October 28

item.title: Nobody won Israel's election — and both sides claimed the mandate anyway
item.description:
Hours after the polls closed, Israel's election produced no winner, only two rival claims to lead the country. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for a "strong, right-wing national government," while challenger Gadi Eisenkot said voters had rejected Netanyahu and called on him to retire from politics. Neither claimed outright victory — because, on every major exit poll, neither bloc has the 61 seats needed to govern.
The numbers barely moved from the evening's exit polls, then tightened further. Reuters reports that revised exit polls from Kan 11 and Channel 13 put the blocs tied at 51–51, while Channel 12 gave Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc a narrow 52–49 edge. With actual votes trickling in, one early-count report put Likud at 25.3% of the vote and Eisenkot's Yashar at 16.6% with about 14% of polling stations counted — early and partial, not a result. Turnout was 77.7%, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee, the highest in more than two decades and about 7 points above 2022. Final results are expected Thursday or Friday.
The two camps read the same deadlock very differently. Netanyahu, speaking after 3 a.m. at Likud headquarters in Jerusalem, framed the moment as a security one: he said Israel faces "a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all," and warned that "ulterior motives must not divert us from this sacred mission." Eisenkot shot back that Netanyahu is "a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people's trust," warned him not to use Israel's security for political purposes, and called on the security establishment to "stand firm" against putting political interests ahead of the country's security. He has also opposed another election, given the high turnout.
The arithmetic is what makes this hard for both men. Netanyahu's nationalist-religious coalition, which at its height held 68 seats, would fall well short of 61, and the far-right religious parties of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich are projected at a combined 13 seats — no major gains for either. Eisenkot's path is blocked from the other side: the Arab parties outside both blocs, projected at 17–19 seats, could hold the balance of power, but Eisenkot has all but ruled out forming a government with them. That leaves him needing support from parties that will not join him, and Netanyahu needing seats he does not have. As Yohanan Plesner of the Israel Democracy Institute put it, the exit polls are a major defeat for Netanyahu's coalition — but Eisenkot has not emerged as a clear winner, and much could change as votes are counted.
For ordinary Israelis, the practical consequence is that Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister while coalition talks drag on — talks that after past elections have run for weeks or months — and if neither bloc can form a government, another vote may be needed. That leaves the unresolved confrontation with Iran, the Gaza aftermath, and Netanyahu's ongoing corruption trial in the hands of a government without a fresh mandate. The Arab parties' surge, driven by record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, is the night's other lasting fact: at the Joint List headquarters in Nazareth, candidates spoke of blocking Netanyahu's return, with candidate Faten Gattas saying, "We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here."
In short: a record-turnout vote, a deadlocked count, and two men claiming a mandate neither holds yet. The next act is not a victory speech but coalition math — and the final results, due Thursday or Friday, could still shift the picture.
Sources: Reuters, October 28; Daily Letter, October 27
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Strikes on Kyiv, a rare call to Putin, and talks booked for Abu Dhabi
item.description:
While Israel counted votes, the war in Ukraine produced a strange pairing on Tuesday: another night of missiles aimed at Kyiv's bridges and logistics, and a rare diplomatic opening — the leaders of Finland and Norway phoning Vladimir Putin to push US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi in early November.
The strikes came first. Reuters reports Russia hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge with ballistic missiles overnight into Tuesday, part of a barrage of up to 16 Iskander-M or S-400 missiles and more than 280 drones, with Kyiv the main target. Mayor Klitschko confirmed the bridge was hit and closed, suspending road and metro traffic between Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir; published images showed a large hole in the deck. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said one person was killed and 15 injured in the capital. Zelensky called it "a serious escalation in Russia's campaign targeting our logistics." The same day's toll spread wider: Russian attacks also caused deaths and injuries in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad, a drone strike on a bus in Moscow-held Zaporizhzhia killed one person and injured 30, and a drone attack on the Russian city of Bryansk killed one and wounded six. Russia's Defence Ministry said it had struck transport infrastructure in Kyiv, a logistics hub in the Kharkiv region, and industrial sites and cargo vessels it said served military purposes. Russia and Ukraine both deny deliberately targeting civilians; Reuters said it could not independently verify the reports.
The diplomacy ran in parallel. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre called Putin from Helsinki on Tuesday to convey messages on future negotiations ahead of the Abu Dhabi meetings, according to a statement from both governments — meetings Kyiv and Moscow agreed on Friday to hold as US-mediated technical talks in early November. Zelensky, who spoke to the pair afterwards, said on X that they had told Putin real steps were needed to de-escalate attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities and infrastructure. Stubb said the war's outcome directly affects the security of Finland and Norway, both of which border Russia, and of Europe more widely: "Ending the war requires direct discussions." The two leaders stressed they acted in their national capacities, not for Europe as a whole, and reaffirmed continued support for Ukraine. The Kremlin's line, as relayed in coverage of the call, is unchanged in substance: any settlement must account for Russia's "legitimate interests," and resuming talks does not restrict ongoing combat operations — a position the strikes on Kyiv the same night did nothing to soften. Some European partners have called the Nordic outreach unilateral, and analysts warn the talks could give Moscow diplomatic cover while military pressure continues.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the two tracks point in opposite directions at once. The bridge closure cuts one of Kyiv's most important Dnipro crossings — road and metro both — with repairs promised but not quick, and the overnight barrage is part of a two-week pattern of concentrated missile strikes on the capital. The Abu Dhabi talks, if they happen, are technical-level meetings, not a peace deal, and the first such US-mediated discussions since February. Meanwhile around Russian-occupied Oleshky, where the local humanitarian ceasefire took effect at 3 a.m. Tuesday, no aid arrival or evacuation had been independently confirmed by Tuesday evening — the wider aid operation is still planned for October 29.
In short: missiles on Kyiv's logistics by night, a phone call to Putin by day, and technical talks booked for early November that neither side has yet allowed to slow the fighting. Watch whether the Oleshky aid operation actually moves on Thursday, and whether Abu Dhabi produces anything beyond a meeting.
Sources: Reuters via Antigua Tribune, October 27; Particle News, October 28; EuropeTimes, October 27
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: antiguatribune.com.

item.title: Houthi/Saudi — Tuesday's barrage, counted two ways
item.description:
The Saudi-led coalition said early Tuesday it intercepted 3 ballistic missiles aimed at the Eastern Region and 4 drones heading south, with no casualties.
By Tuesday evening, the Levant Files' live coverage, citing Al Jazeera Arabic, put the day's total at 5 ballistic missiles and 4 drones intercepted, with falling debris causing material damage in Riyadh and civil defence alerts lifted across six locations including Riyadh, Najran, Khamis Mushait and Abha. The counts differ by source and time of day — treat them as a developing tally, not a settled one.
The coalition also said it struck Houthi positions in Yemen, destroying launchers, storage tunnels and a missile depot; that claim is unverified. No new Houthi claim beyond Tuesday's Ras Tanura refinery claim, already reported in the evening brief, surfaced by late Tuesday CT.
Sources: Muslim Network TV, October 27;
Source: muslimnetwork.tv.

item.title: Google DeepMind shows Genie 4, a world model with sound
item.description:
Google DeepMind announced Genie 4 on Tuesday: a real-time world model that generates ambient audio natively — wind, waves, and characters that talk and react — with scenes editable by plain text and Gemini guiding generation as an agent.
It is a research preview for trusted testers, coming to Project Genie for Google AI Ultra subscribers and to early-access partners via the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, with no date given and no figures for resolution, frame rate or session length. Not a consumer launch yet, but it is Google's biggest AI-model announcement of the week.
Source:
Source: thehype.news.

item.title: CISA adds the Brotli flaw to its exploited list
item.description:
CVE-2026-111497 — the out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli compression decoder, CVSS 9.2 — joined CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27, with a federal remediation deadline of November 10.
This is a step up from its status as of October 26, when it was flagged as a serious flaw with public proof-of-concept code but not yet listed as exploited. Fixes are in Brotli 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1.
It joins the Adobe Commerce/Magento flaw (CVE-2026-48356, also due November 10) added the same day and reported in the evening brief. Source:
Source: securityonline.info.

item.title: Israel votes — and nobody wins: exit polls point to deadlock
item.description:
Israelis voted Tuesday in their first election since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks, and the exit polls say the country is split almost exactly down the middle. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor challenger Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc is projected to reach the 61 seats needed to govern, setting up days or weeks of coalition wrangling — and possibly another election.
Turnout was the story of the day before any seat count: USA Today reports at least 80% of eligible voters cast ballots, a record high, with 74.3% already counted by 8 p.m. local time, two hours before polls closed. The exit polls published after voting ended were strikingly consistent across the major broadcasters. Channel 12 put Netanyahu's bloc at 50 seats and Eisenkot's bloc at 52; the Kan public broadcaster had it 50–53. Likud remains the largest single party at 24–25 seats, ahead of Eisenkot's Yashar at 21–23 — but a bloc, not a party, forms a government. The big mover was the Arab-led parties, projected at 17 seats, up sharply, making them potentially decisive in coalition talks. One outlier broke the pattern: Channel 14, a network generally supportive of Netanyahu, projected his bloc at 60 seats and Eisenkot's at 43, with Likud at 30 — a reminder that exit polls are projections, not results, and the picture can shift as votes are counted overnight.
The two camps read the same numbers very differently. Eisenkot said in a statement: "If these are the final results, they would mark a victory." Fellow opposition leader Yair Lapid went further, calling it a "total collapse" for Netanyahu's bloc and saying "the public told them to go home." Netanyahu, who voted in Jerusalem with his wife Sara, spent the day warning supporters that the election was being stolen, pointing to the arrests of three men in the Negev suspected of trying to buy votes for the Islamist Ra'am party, with investigators finding envelopes of tens of thousands of shekels and ballot slips. He also appealed urgently as reports emerged of unusually high turnout among Arab voters. Eisenkot's camp, by contrast, framed the vote as a verdict on the government of October 7 and the failure to establish an independent commission of inquiry.
For ordinary Israelis, the immediate consequence is uncertainty, not a new government. If neither bloc reaches 61, leaders must court smaller parties outside their coalitions — including the Arab parties — or Netanyahu could remain as caretaker prime minister while talks drag on. Preliminary results are due as early as Wednesday, and the coalition math, not the vote count alone, will decide who governs through the unresolved confrontation with Iran, the Gaza aftermath, and Netanyahu's ongoing corruption trial.
In short: a record-turnout vote that changed the balance — Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority, Eisenkot's bloc edged ahead — but gave nobody a government. The next act is coalition negotiation, with the Arab parties holding unusual leverage.
Sources: USA Today, October 27; Algemeiner, October 27; New York Post, October 27; The Sun, October 27
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*

item.title: Houthis claim a missile hit Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery — as Tehran talks and oil markets pull in opposite directions
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis said Tuesday they hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery — the kingdom's largest — with a ballistic missile, while diplomats from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were in Tehran trying to de-escalate the wider regional war. Oil fell on the diplomacy, but stayed near six-month highs on the attacks.
Reuters reports Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the strike caused a fire at the Ras Tanura complex, which includes a shipping terminal on the Gulf and refines 550,000 barrels a day. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike. Bloomberg News, cited by Reuters, reported a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura's terminal in the early hours. The Houthis also claimed attacks on two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an air base in Khamis Mushait — neither confirmed by Riyadh. Separately, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh, and civil defence authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the capital Tuesday afternoon. On Monday, the Mecca defence pact countries — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — met Iranian officials in Tehran to try to de-escalate the overall conflict, and on Tuesday Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei; Iranian state media said the four countries agreed to continue talks on peace and security.
The two sides' accounts diverge in the usual way: the Houthis present the refinery strike as a direct hit with a fire; Riyadh has not confirmed it, and the Bloomberg-sourced account describes a contained fire near the terminal rather than a refinery outage. What is not in dispute is the pattern — Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil installations have intensified since September, and nearly all Saudi oil exports flow through Ras Tanura and the Red Sea port of Yanbu, both previously attacked. Market analysts at Gelber & Associates put it plainly: "Continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the expanding military presence in the Gulf are keeping supply risks in place, even as diplomatic headlines encourage some of the recent premium to unwind."
For ordinary people, the price signal is the one that reaches the pump. Reuters reports Brent crude settled down $1.93, or 1.67%, at $113.88 a barrel on Tuesday, with US West Texas Intermediate down $1.86 at $99.90 — a pullback on the Tehran talks, but still near six-month highs. Swiss bank UBS now expects Brent to stay elevated near $110 through year-end, up from a previous $100 forecast. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways since a Washington think tank began tracking maritime incidents in 2017.
In short: a claimed strike on the kingdom's biggest refinery, an unconfirmed but contained fire, missiles intercepted over Riyadh — and, in parallel, the first real diplomatic channel in weeks. Oil eased on the talks but is not coming down while the attacks continue.
Sources: Reuters via WNCY, October 27; Reuters via Devdiscourse, October 27; Reuters via Euronext, October 27

item.title: Oracle expands Nvidia deal to "multi-gigawatt scale" — and starts offering Google's TPUs
item.description:
Reuters reports Oracle said Tuesday it will expand its cloud AI chip deal with Nvidia's newest Vera Rubin servers to multi-gigawatt scale (no value disclosed; Nvidia's Jensen Huang has previously said Vera Rubin systems can generate up to $40 billion per gigawatt for Nvidia).
The notable twist: Oracle will skip some Nvidia networking chips in favor of its own in-house "Acceleron" chips, and will begin offering Google's tensor processing units for the first time, alongside inference chips from Cerebras and Intel-backed SambaNova. Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman called it "a massive expansion of our customer base of tier-one customers."
The read: even Nvidia's biggest cloud customers are diversifying, especially for inference, where Nvidia's grip is looser than in training. Source:
Source: wtbx.com.

item.title: Apple's touchscreen Mac event is Wednesday — what to expect
item.description:
Apple's "Pro and tell" event in Los Angeles starts 10 a.m.
Pacific Wednesday. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros with touch-enabled OLED displays — a first for any Mac — plus a Dynamic Island replacing the notch, lighter builds, and the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips from March rather than new silicon.
Pricing could run up to $500 above current models ($2,499 for 14-inch, $2,999 for 16-inch). macOS Golden Gate is said to add a "dynamic interface" that adapts controls based on whether you're touching the screen or using the trackpad. The M6 14-inch MacBook Pro ($1,999) and iMac ($1,499) from Tuesday remain the conventional options, on sale November 6.
Sources: MacRumors, October 25;

item.title: Brand trial: judge downgrades one charge as prosecution nears its end — and a correction to this morning
item.description:
Tuesday at Southwark Crown Court, jurors heard four pre-prepared police statements from Russell Brand (2023–2025) in which he said he had "never engaged in any non-consensual sexual activity," describing a "very promiscuous" past and saying 2023 media reports had "reframed" consensual encounters.
Mr Justice Bennathan then told jurors there was insufficient evidence on the indecent assault count (the alleged 2001 MTV incident) and directed a not-guilty verdict on it; the indictment was amended to attempted indecent assault, to which Brand has pleaded not guilty. He now faces three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault over allegations from 1999–2009.
The prosecution is due to finish Wednesday morning, after which the defence opens. Correction to the morning brief: Brand has not yet given evidence in person — Tuesday's material was his police statements read to the court, and whether he testifies himself remains unconfirmed.
Sources: Reuters via WTBX, October 27;
Source: wtbx.com.

item.title: A truce begins in Oleshky — while Kyiv takes another night of missiles
item.description:
A rare local ceasefire has begun in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, even as Russia pounded Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities overnight. The two facts sitting side by side are the story: a humanitarian pause in one town, and no pause anywhere else.
Reuters reports that both sides confirmed the Oleshky ceasefire on Tuesday morning. Russia's defence ministry said it stopped shelling toward the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson from 4 a.m. Moscow time (0100 GMT), and Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on Facebook that "the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments." The deal, coordinated with US First Lady Melania Trump and Russia's human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, is meant to let food, water and medicine into a town where up to 2,000 civilians remain, many elderly or with limited mobility, and to prepare evacuations. A wider humanitarian operation is planned to start on October 29, according to a summary of the arrangement. The ceasefire covers only the Oleshky area — it is not a wider truce, and neither side has said who monitors it.
At the same time, Reuters reports new strikes on Tuesday hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge and subway infrastructure, forcing traffic to halt, while a Reuters witness heard explosions. Ukraine's Air Force said the overnight assault, running from 6 p.m. Monday, used Iskander-M and S-400 ballistic missiles plus 280 strike drones, with Kyiv the main direction of attack. By 9 a.m., air defences had destroyed or suppressed 257 targets — two ballistic missiles and 255 drones — with hits recorded at 25 locations and debris falling at 16 more. President Volodymyr Zelensky said 16 ballistic missiles were launched in total, the injured from the university-campus strike had risen to 12, and strikes also hit the Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Kherson and Chernivtsi regions.
The two sides describe the Kyiv strikes in entirely different terms. Zelensky called the bridge strike "a serious escalation in Russia's operation against our logistics" and renewed his attack on delays to Patriot and NASAMS interceptor deliveries, saying "every such delay means another Russian strike on one facility or another." Moscow's defence ministry said it hit transport infrastructure in Kyiv, a logistics hub in the Kharkiv region, and industrial facilities and cargo vessels it said were put to military use. Reuters notes it could not independently verify the reports, and both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians. Casualty figures are still moving: Reuters' Tuesday wire puts the Kyiv toll since Monday evening at at least one killed and 15 injured, including students in a dormitory, while Zelensky's Tuesday statement put the injured at 12; people were also killed and injured in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad, and a drone attack killed a man in the Russian city of Bryansk.
For ordinary people, the practical effects are immediate and concrete. Kyiv commuters lost a main Dnipro crossing and metro service on the bridge section on Tuesday morning, on top of a night of sirens and explosions; in Oleshky, the question is whether aid trucks and evacuation routes actually move in the coming days, after years in which mined roads and drone attacks made leaving dangerous. The truce's first test is delivery, not declaration.
In short: Oleshky's humanitarian pause is real and confirmed by both sides, but it is narrow, unmonitored in any published detail, and surrounded by a war that escalated overnight — with Kyiv's bridge and metro hit, and Ukraine's parliament voting to extend the war footing into next year.
Sources: Reuters via WTBX, October 27; TBS News, October 27; Kyiv24 / Ukrainian Air Force, October 27; ANI via Daily Prabhat, October 27
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: wtbx.com.

item.title: Israelis vote in their first election since October 7 — and neither bloc looks set to win it
item.description:
Israelis are voting Tuesday in a parliamentary election that is, above all, a verdict on Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership after three years of war — and one that, on the final polls, neither side is projected to win outright.
Polls opened at 7 a.m. local time for about 7.3 million eligible voters choosing the 120-seat Knesset, with voting running until 10 p.m. and exit polls expected shortly after. The contest pits Netanyahu's Likud and its right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies against an opposition alliance led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar party. Final television-network polls put Yashar ahead of Likud, roughly 22–23 seats to 19–21, but Netanyahu's bloc at about 50 seats and the main opposition bloc at 52–56 — both short of the 61 needed for a majority, with Arab-led parties projected at 14–16 seats and therefore potentially decisive in coalition talks.
The two campaigns are arguing about different things, and that is the point of disagreement. Eisenkot, whose son died in Gaza in December 2023 and who quit the wartime cabinet in June 2024, opened election day by invoking the October 7, 2023 Hamas massacre, posting: "Today we have an opportunity to put a slip in the ballot box, to replace the government of October 7th." His bloc is demanding accountability for the failures around the attacks and an independent commission of inquiry, and casting Netanyahu as dangerous for Israel's security. Netanyahu, by contrast, is campaigning on his wartime leadership, his alliance with President Trump — who has endorsed him — and a strong-man image, with Likud billboards carrying the slogan "Right or Palestine." item.content:encoded:
Israelis are voting Tuesday in a parliamentary election that is, above all, a verdict on Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership after three years of war — and one that, on the final polls, neither side is projected to win outright.

Polls opened at 7 a.m. local time for about 7.3 million eligible voters choosing the 120-seat Knesset, with voting running until 10 p.m. and exit polls expected shortly after. The contest pits Netanyahu's Likud and its right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies against an opposition alliance led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar party. Final television-network polls put Yashar ahead of Likud, roughly 22–23 seats to 19–21, but Netanyahu's bloc at about 50 seats and the main opposition bloc at 52–56 — both short of the 61 needed for a majority, with Arab-led parties projected at 14–16 seats and therefore potentially decisive in coalition talks.

The two campaigns are arguing about different things, and that is the point of disagreement. Eisenkot, whose son died in Gaza in December 2023 and who quit the wartime cabinet in June 2024, opened election day by invoking the October 7, 2023 Hamas massacre, posting: "Today we have an opportunity to put a slip in the ballot box, to replace the government of October 7th." His bloc is demanding accountability for the failures around the attacks and an independent commission of inquiry, and casting Netanyahu as dangerous for Israel's security. Netanyahu, by contrast, is campaigning on his wartime leadership, his alliance with President Trump — who has endorsed him — and a strong-man image, with Likud billboards carrying the slogan "Right or Palestine." Eisenkot counters that Trump would work with any leader voters choose. On policy, the gap is narrower than the rhetoric: Eisenkot shares some of Netanyahu's positions on the conflict, and the sharpest divides are over accountability, ultra-Orthodox military-service exemptions, and who should answer for October 7.

For ordinary Israelis, the stakes are who governs through the unresolved confrontation with Iran, the aftermath of the Gaza war, and the corruption trial still hanging over Netanyahu — plus an independent UN inquiry report reaffirming allegations of grave abuses in Gaza, issued the day before voting. If neither bloc reaches 61, coalition negotiations with smaller and Arab parties will decide the government, and Netanyahu could remain as caretaker if no coalition forms.

In short: a close, high-stakes vote with no projected winner — the result will be decided less by who gets the most votes than by who can build 61 seats afterwards, with exit polls due Tuesday night local time.

item.title: Apple launches the M6 MacBook Pro and iMac — a day before its touchscreen Mac event
item.description:
Apple on Tuesday unveiled a new 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac powered by its M6 chip, pitching faster on-device AI — the second day of a product rollout that peaks Wednesday with its "Pro and tell" event in Los Angeles.
Reuters reports the 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 and the iMac at $1,499, with pre-orders opening Wednesday in 35 countries and regions and availability starting November 6. Apple says the M6 MacBook Pro delivers up to 30% faster graphics and up to 25% faster AI performance than its M5 predecessor, with up to 24 hours of battery life — the longest ever in a Mac — while the new iMac delivers up to 5x faster on-device AI performance than the previous M4 model. Pocket-lint adds the context that matters for buyers: the MacBook Pro jump is modest because the 14-inch model already ran M5, while the iMac jump is bigger because Apple last refreshed it in 2024 with M4. MacRumors adds the specs: a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, Wi-Fi 7, 16GB of unified memory and 1TB of storage as standard on the MacBook Pro, in Space Black and Silver, configurable up to 32GB and 4TB.
The timing is the other half of the story. The launches come a day before Apple's October 28 event, which Bloomberg has reported will feature Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro — a product Apple executives once publicly dismissed, with Steve Jobs calling touchscreen laptops "ergonomically terrible" and Tim Cook comparing a Mac-iPad merge to "combining a toaster and a refrigerator." Apple is expected to frame touch as a secondary input — scrolling, zooming, panning — with keyboard and trackpad remaining primary. The M6 refresh is deliberately limited to the 14-inch MacBook Pro, Pocket-lint notes, because the touchscreen model is expected to take the spotlight tomorrow.
For buyers, the practical read is simple: if you want a conventional MacBook Pro or an iMac, the M6 models are the new baseline from November 6; if you want a touchscreen Mac, wait one more day before deciding, because tomorrow's announcement may change the lineup and pricing picture.
In short: a solid, AI-pitched M6 refresh for the 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac, priced at $1,999 and $1,499, landing November 6 — and clearly staged as the warm-up act for Wednesday's touchscreen Mac reveal.
Sources: Reuters, October 27; Pocket-lint, October 27; MacRumors, October 27
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Nvidia puts $3 billion into Meta's giant AI fundraising as the two deepen their Muse partnership
item.description:
Nvidia and Meta on Tuesday deepened their partnership around Meta's Muse AI assistant and models, with Nvidia investing $3 billion in Meta's equity offering — a chipmaker buying into its biggest customer's AI buildout.
Reuters reports the two companies will work more closely to improve Muse's training and inference performance and reduce costs, with Muse — known internally as Hatch — central to CEO Mark Zuckerberg's plan to deliver "personal superintelligence" to the billions of people who use Meta's services daily. Dow Jones adds that Meta intends to increase deployment of Nvidia infrastructure, including Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs, for next-generation AI agents, and that the companies may also work together on monitoring agent behavior. The deal sits inside Meta's enormous fundraising: Meta increased its equity offering to $97.5 billion, the largest in its history, to bankroll AI infrastructure spending, after initially announcing roughly $35 billion in tranches and then upsizing. Nvidia's $3 billion is a slice of that, not a takeover — no purchase price, share count or ownership percentage was disclosed.
The two sides frame the deal differently, and both framings matter. For Meta, it is about securing compute and credibility for an agent — modeled on the open-source OpenClaw — that can access a user's email, calendar, payments, health, shopping and smart-home apps, with users able to revoke access at any time. For Nvidia, it is about locking its Vera Rubin platform, Spectrum-X Ethernet and BlueField-4 networking into Meta's data centers, plus a possible role for its OpenShell framework and Sentry agent-monitoring tool in how Muse agents are rolled out safely. Critics of this kind of circular AI financing — a supplier funding its customer's spending — will note the structure; supporters will note Meta is also raising tens of billions from public markets, not just from Nvidia.
For ordinary users, the near-term effect is not a new product but a bet: Meta's AI assistant gets more Nvidia hardware behind it, and the companies are explicitly tying the partnership to agents that act across your apps — which makes the access controls and monitoring they mention worth watching as closely as the speed claims.
In short: Nvidia buys $3 billion into Meta's record $97.5 billion raise, Meta buys deeper into Nvidia's Vera Rubin stack, and Muse — Meta's agent bet — is the product both sides are really investing in.
Sources: Reuters via KWSN, October 27; Dow Jones via Morningstar, October 27; TradingKey, October 27
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved from the article pages checked, so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: kwsn.com.

item.title: PHP2Shell fallout widens — new scale, not a new flaw
item.description:
The two critical PHP flaws added to CISA's exploited list Monday (CVE-2026-109618/109619, CVSS 9.2, federal deadline October 29) are now backed by fresh scale reporting: Censys counts 32.51 million affected services, Cloudflare logged millions of exploitation attempts, Check Point says 10% of organizations worldwide were impacted, and some attacks dropped the Potassium Mirai variant.
Fixed releases remain PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35; older branches get no patch. This is an update to Monday night's KEV item, not a new vulnerability.
Sources: Softonic, October 27;
Source: en.softonic.com.

item.title: Kyiv hit by ballistic missiles hours before the Oleshky truce was due to start
item.description:
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv late Monday evening, hitting a university campus, a metro-station area, homes and medical facilities — just hours before a local humanitarian truce was due to begin in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. It is a developing story, and the casualty count is still moving.
Reuters reports that at least one person was killed and 10 injured, many of them outside a student dormitory at the State Trade and Economics University on the east side of the Dnipro River. Nine people were in hospital, three of them in serious condition, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. The Guardian's briefing, published later, put the wounded at eight and said medical facilities and an intensive care unit were damaged — a reminder that the toll is not yet settled. A second wave of missiles was reported in the middle of the night, hitting an administrative building in the Podilskyi district, according to the Kyiv Independent via Europe Says, with the full consequences still unclear.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the missiles hit "very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby," calling it "a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure." Moscow has long denied targeting civilians, and Russia has not commented on this specific strike in the coverage checked. Zelensky also used the attack to press his air-defence argument again: he said Ukraine has been waiting nearly a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, and that "artificial delays in air defence for Ukraine are helping terror."
For ordinary people in Kyiv, a city of about three million, this is the pattern of recent weeks: sirens and explosions at night, power cut in districts east of the Dnipro, and now a university dormitory and hospital wards in the damage reports. Paramedics were among the injured — two emergency crew members were hurt rushing to one strike scene, Klitschko said.
The timing is what makes this strike land harder than a routine nightly barrage. The Oleshky truce, agreed last Friday, was due to begin at 3 a.m. local time Tuesday (0100 GMT), to let food, medicine and evacuations reach a town occupied since 2022 where only a few thousand of its 24,000 prewar residents remain. According to the Guardian, no end date has been given, and neither Russia, Ukraine nor the US has said who would monitor it or given details of the humanitarian operation. Russia's defence ministry said Friday it would halt fire in the "Kherson sector" for the duration of the ceasefire; Ukraine has accused Russia of blocking residents from leaving, a charge Moscow denies. As of this brief, there is no confirmation in the coverage checked that the truce is holding — that is the first thing to check in the morning.
In short: a deadly strike on civilian Kyiv on the eve of a fragile local truce, with air-defence supplies still the argument in Kyiv and Washington — and Oleshky's first hours under the truce unconfirmed.
Sources: Reuters via SRN News, October 26; Guardian war briefing via Stocks99, October 27; Kyiv Independent via Europe Says, October 26–27
*Note on images: no clean lead image could be retrieved for this article — the Reuters-carrying page offered only a loader graphic — so none is included rather than a guessed one.*
Source: srnnews.com.

item.title: Romania: Russia-linked arson network alleged
item.description:
Romania said Monday that a network "coordinated" from Russia was involved in starting a fire on September 14 near an arms factory in Brasov; two Belarusians and a Ukrainian, residents in EU countries, were involved, two were tracked down and remanded in Germany while preparing similar offences, and a third is at large in Poland, according to Romania's organised-crime office.
Russia's embassy in Bucharest could not immediately be reached for comment, and Moscow has repeatedly denied such accusations. The Guardian briefing also notes at least eight cargo ships hit off NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks, with some 34 sailors reported dead or missing — part of what NATO and the EU describe as a Russian hybrid campaign, which Moscow denies.
Source:
Source: stocks99.in.

item.title: Israel votes Tuesday
item.description:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival, Reuters reports, with voters weighing his leadership after the 2023 Hamas-led attacks and the wars in Gaza and with Iran.
Polls show a close race between Netanyahu's Likud and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Netanyahu is campaigning on his wartime leadership and his alliance with President Trump, who has endorsed him; Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of "fear-mongering, lies and threats" and says Trump would work with any leader chosen by voters.
Neither side has a clear path to a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Reuters notes — if neither can form one, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election next year. Polls open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time Tuesday.
Source:
Source: 935thelloyd.com.

item.title: Hallmark trending on GitHub
item.description:
Nutlope/hallmark, an "anti-AI-slop" design skill for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex, gained about 2,200 stars in 24 hours on October 26, according to GitDiscover's trending tracker — a sign of how much developer attention is going to design quality in AI-generated interfaces, not just code output.
Source:
Source: gitdiscover.org.

item.title: CISA adds two critical PHP flaws to its exploited list — federal deadline October 29
item.description:
CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26, SSJ News reports.
Both are unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaws in PHP's web-serving configurations, rated CVSS 9.2, with fixed releases PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 (PHP 8.1 and earlier get no patches). CISA's updated alert directs organizations that cannot update immediately, or still run unsupported versions, to take PHP-based systems offline until they can be patched.
This escalates the PHP2Shell flaws already reported Monday morning from "reported exploited" to formally listed as exploited with a federal deadline. Source:
Source: ssj.news.

item.title: State Bank of India breach disclosed
item.description:
India's state-run State Bank of India, serving more than 500 million customers, disclosed a data breach after 3,897 customer records appeared online, Check Point Research reports in its October 26 threat report.
Exposed information reportedly included contact details, residential addresses, birth dates, bank profiles, loan records and identity-verification documents. The bank reported no disruption to core services.
Source:
Source: research.checkpoint.com.
